metadata.title: Lean formalization of opinion dynamics and related processes.

nodes.name: Round randomness
nodes.statement: A \emph{round configuration} is a function $r \colon V \to V \times V \times V$ assigning to every agent $v$ an ordered triple of \emph{samples}, each drawn independently and uniformly from $V$, \emph{with} replacement (an agent may sample itself, or the same agent twice --- harmless, since a majority of three Boolean values is always well defined). Let $R_n = V^{3V}$ denote the (finite) set of round configurations, with the uniform probability measure.
nodes.label: def:round

nodes.name: Majority step
nodes.statement: For an opinion-$1$ set $I \subseteq V$ and $r \in R_n$, \[ \mathrm{step}(I,r) \;=\; \{\, v \in V : \text{at least two of } r(v)\text{'s three coordinates lie in } I \,\}. \] Each agent independently samples $3$ agents and adopts the majority of their current opinions.
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Process
nodes.statement: Fix a horizon $T \in \N$ and an initial set $I_0 \subseteq V$. The sample space is $\Omega = R_n^{\,T}$ with the uniform (i.i.d.) measure. For $r = (r_0,\dots,r_{T-1}) \in \Omega$ define $I_{t+1} = \mathrm{step}(I_t, r_t)$. We write $X_t = |I_t|$ and $U_t = n - X_t$. In the formalization, a trajectory is a \texttt{List} of round configurations and $\mathrm{run}\ I\ l$ folds \texttt{step} over the list $l$.
nodes.label: def:process

nodes.name: Monotone coupling
nodes.statement: For a \emph{fixed} round $r$, the map $I \mapsto \mathrm{step}(I,r)$ is monotone: $I \subseteq I'$ implies $\mathrm{step}(I,r) \subseteq \mathrm{step}(I',r)$; iterating over a trajectory, $\mathrm{run}$ is monotone in the same sense. This is purely combinatorial (no probability involved).
nodes.label: lem:mono

nodes.statement: Unlike the push protocol, where the analogous monotonicity (Lemma~\ref{lem:mono} there) is load-bearing throughout, here the per-round probabilistic estimates below (Lemmas~\ref{lem:growthround}, \ref{lem:satclosed}, etc.) are instead stated and proved directly for \emph{any} set $I$ satisfying a hypothesis on $|I|$, using monotonicity of the real polynomial $p$ of Section~\ref{sec:map} on $[0,1]$ rather than a reference-embedding argument via Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}. Lemma~\ref{lem:mono} is recorded because it is the exact analogue of the push protocol's structural fact, but it is not otherwise used by the chain of lemmas leading to the main theorem.

nodes.name: 3-majority reaches consensus in $O(\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be such that $\log n \ge 30$ (in particular $n \ge 2$), let $I_0 \subseteq V$ with $|I_0| \ge \tfrac35 n$, and set \[ T \;=\; 10 + (T_{2a}(n) + 2), \qquad T_{2a}(n) = \ceil{6\log n}. \] Then $\Pr[\, I_T = V \,] \;\ge\; 1 - \dfrac{500}{n}$.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.statement: As in the push protocol's write-up, the threshold $\log n \ge 30$ and the constant $500$ are deliberately crude: the proof is organized to keep every inequality an easy direct computation, not to be sharp. Reaching this modest, two-digit threshold on $\log n$ (rather than an astronomically large one) relies on two ingredients in Section~\ref{sec:ineq}: a degree-$11$ instance of the generic exponential-vs-power bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:exppow}), and a log-log bound tangent at a reference point near the threshold itself rather than at the fixed point $e$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:loglog}). It is known (Doerr--Goldberg--Minder--Sauerwald--Scheideler 2011; Becchetti--Clementi--Natale--Pasquale--Silvestri, SODA 2015) that an initial imbalance of only $\Theta(\sqrt{n\log n})$ already suffices for $O(\log n)$-round consensus w.h.p.; reaching that sharp threshold requires tracking the process on the scale of its own standard deviation throughout, a substantially more delicate multi-scale argument. Here a constant-fraction initial imbalance keeps every step to a single, reusable Chernoff bound (Section~\ref{sec:chernoff}) applied at a handful of explicit parameters.

nodes.name: Average
nodes.statement: For a finite type $\alpha$ and $f \colon \alpha \to \R$, $\mathrm{avg}(f) := \bigl(\sum_a f(a)\bigr)/|\alpha|$ is the expectation of $f$ under the uniform distribution on $\alpha$.
nodes.label: def:avg

nodes.name: Trajectory expectation
nodes.statement: Exactly as in the push protocol: $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ F$ is the expectation of a functional $F$ of a trajectory of $T$ i.i.d.\ uniform draws from $\alpha$, defined by recursion on $T$ (the head draw is averaged out first), so conditioning on the first round is a definitional unfolding.
nodes.label: def:expList

nodes.name: Basic properties
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{avg}$ and $\mathrm{expList}$ are monotone, additive, homogeneous, and constants pass through unchanged; $\mathrm{expList}$ over a concatenated horizon splits as a nested $\mathrm{expList}$ (\texttt{expList\_append}), used to glue phases in Section~\ref{sec:proof-main}.
nodes.label: lem:avg-basic

nodes.name: Independence over a product space
nodes.statement: \textbf{New relative to the push protocol}, since that development only ever averaged over a single uniform draw at a time. For finite types $\beta,\delta$ and $g \colon \beta\to\R$, $h\colon\delta\to\R$: $\mathrm{avg}(p \mapsto g(p_1)h(p_2)) = \mathrm{avg}(g)\,\mathrm{avg}(h)$ over the product $\beta\times\delta$ (\texttt{avg\_mul\_prod}), with marginal consequences \texttt{avg\_fst\_mul}/\texttt{avg\_snd\_mul}. Iterating over a $\mathrm{Fin}\ n$-indexed product (\texttt{avg\_prod\_pi}): for $f \colon \mathrm{Fin}\ n \to \gamma \to \R$, \[ \mathrm{avg}\Bigl(x \mapsto \textstyle\prod_i f_i(x_i)\Bigr) \;=\; \prod_i \mathrm{avg}(f_i) \] over $x \colon \mathrm{Fin}\ n \to \gamma$ --- the discrete, measure-theory-free form of ``coordinate projections on a product space are independent,'' with a one-coordinate marginal corollary (\texttt{avg\_eval}). This is exactly the independence fact that lets the $n$ agents' per-round updates be combined into a single concentration bound (Section~\ref{sec:chernoff}).
nodes.label: lem:indep

nodes.name: Majority-of-three as a polynomial
nodes.statement: For $a,b,c \in \{0,1\}$: $\mathbf 1[a+b+c\ge2] = ab+bc+ac-2abc$. Applied pointwise to the three samples of a fixed agent, this expresses the majority indicator as a polynomial in the three membership indicators.
nodes.label: lem:majpoly

nodes.name: Per-agent contribution
nodes.statement: $Y_{\mathrm{maj}}(I,v,s) \in \{0,1\}$ is $1$ iff a majority of the sample triple $s$ lies in $I$ (independent of $v$, kept as a function of $v$ to match the shape the Chernoff bound of Section~\ref{sec:chernoff} expects). Then $|\mathrm{step}(I,r)| = \sum_v Y_{\mathrm{maj}}(I,v,r(v))$ (\texttt{card\_step\_eq\_sum}): the per-agent, $\{0,1\}$-valued decomposition that Section~\ref{sec:chernoff}'s tail bounds need.
nodes.label: def:Ymaj

nodes.name: Exact one-round drift
nodes.statement: Conditionally on a fixed $I$ with $|I|=m$, the next count $X_{t+1} = |\mathrm{step}(I,r)|$ satisfies \[ \E_r[X_{t+1}] \;=\; n\,p(x), \qquad p(x) := 3x^2-2x^3, \qquad x = m/n, \] proved exactly (no approximation) via Lemma~\ref{lem:majpoly}, Definition~\ref{def:Ymaj} and the independence toolkit of Lemma~\ref{lem:indep} (each pairwise/triple product of membership indicators over distinct coordinates of the product space $\mathrm{Tgt3}\ n$ factors by \texttt{avg\_mul\_prod}).
nodes.label: lem:drift

nodes.name: Dissent contribution
nodes.statement: $Y_{\mathrm{dis}} := 1 - Y_{\mathrm{maj}}$, the complementary per-agent dissent contribution, so $n - |\mathrm{step}(I,r)| = \sum_v Y_{\mathrm{dis}}(I,v,r(v))$ with mean $n - n\,p(x)$ (\texttt{sum\_avg\_Y\_dis}); by the algebraic identity $1-p(x) = (1-x)^2(1+2x)$ this is the quantity controlled in Section~\ref{sec:saturation}.
nodes.label: def:Ydis

nodes.statement: The algebraic identities for $p$ used throughout below --- $p(x)-x = x(1-x)(2x-1)$, $1-p(x) = (1-x)^2(1+2x)$, and the growth/saturation regional bounds $p(\tfrac12+\beta)-\tfrac12 \ge \tfrac54\beta$ for $0\le\beta\le\tfrac14$ and $u(3-2u)\le\tfrac58$ for $0\le u\le\tfrac14$ --- are not isolated as separate Lean lemmas: each use site (\texttt{growth\_round}, \texttt{saturation\_round\_closed}, \texttt{saturation\_mean\_quad}) re-derives the specific polynomial inequality it needs inline via \texttt{ring}/\texttt{nlinarith}, in the same spirit as the push protocol's reverse-Markov bound, which is also not isolated as its own named lemma.

nodes.name: Quadratic-tight logarithm bound
nodes.statement: For $\tfrac12 \le x \le 1$: $(x-1)-(x-1)^2 \le \log x$. (Mathlib's crude linear bound $\log x \ge x-1$ is false for $x<1$ and, worse, plugging the correct one-sided bound $1-\tfrac1x\le\log x$ into the Chernoff exponent $k-\mu-k\log(k/\mu)$ gives exactly $0$ when $k/\mu\to1$ --- useless. This quadratic correction, derived from Mathlib's degree-$3$ Taylor lower bound for $\exp$ by elementary algebra, is what makes the growth-phase Chernoff bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:growthround}) bite.)
nodes.label: lem:logquad

nodes.name: Exponential beats any fixed power
nodes.statement: For $x\ge0$ and any $k\in\N$: $x^k/k! \le \exp(x)$ --- the single degree-$k$ term of the Taylor truncation, extracted by dropping every other (nonnegative, since $x\ge0$) term of the sum. The cubic case $k=3$ (\texttt{exp\_ge\_cube}) is the special case used by Lemma~\ref{lem:logquad}. Choosing $k$ large enough relative to a given lower bound on $\log n$ lets $n$ be shown to dominate any fixed polynomial in $\log n$ using only a \emph{modest} such lower bound (Stage 2b, Lemma~\ref{lem:stage2b}, and the final numeric bound Lemma~\ref{lem:mainfailclean}) --- a single low-degree truncation, such as the cubic case alone, would instead force $\log n$ to be astronomically large.
nodes.label: lem:exppow

nodes.name: Tangent-line log bound
nodes.statement: For $L>0$ and any reference point $c>0$: $\log L \le \log c - 1 + L/c$, from the crude bound $\log t \le t - 1$ applied to $t = L/c$; tight at $L=c$ (equality there), unlike a bound tangent at a single globally-fixed point, so choosing $c$ near the $L$ actually in play gives a far sharper bound. Also records $\exp(3)\ge20$ (cubing the standard $10$-digit lower bound on $e$), used to instantiate $c=\exp(3)$ below.
nodes.label: lem:logtangent

nodes.name: Log-log bound
nodes.statement: For $\log x>0$: $\log\log x \le 2 + (\log x)/20$, from Lemma~\ref{lem:logtangent} tangent at the reference point $c=\exp(3)\approx20.09$ (so $\log c = 3$ exactly), combined with $\exp(3)\ge20$ to replace $1/\exp(3)$ by the cruder but rational $1/20$. Far tighter, once $\log x$ is more than a few units above $e$, than a bound tangent at the fixed point $c=e$ (the crude bound $\log t\le t-1$ applied directly at $t=(\log x)/e$) --- exactly the regime Lemma~\ref{lem:stage2b} needs. Used only inside Lemma~\ref{lem:stage2b}'s numeric estimate.
nodes.label: lem:loglog

nodes.name: MGF bound
nodes.statement: Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n \colon \gamma \to \{0,1\}$ be the per-agent contributions on the product space $\mathrm{Fin}\ n \to \gamma$ (one independent draw of $\gamma$ per agent), with $\mu=\sum_i\mathrm{avg}(Y_i)$ and $X(x) := \sum_i Y_i(x_i)$. Then for every real $t$ (no sign restriction): \[ \E[\exp(tX)] \;\le\; \exp\bigl(\mu(e^t-1)\bigr). \] Proved via the independence toolkit (Lemma~\ref{lem:indep}) applied to $x \mapsto \prod_i \exp(tY_i(x_i))$, and the elementary bound $1+y\le e^y$ (Mathlib's \texttt{Real.add\_one\_le\_exp}) at each factor.
nodes.label: lem:mgf

nodes.name: Chernoff tail bounds
nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:mgf}: for $t\ge0$ and any $k$, $\Pr[X\ge k] \le \exp(\mu(e^t-1)-tk)$ (\texttt{avg\_chernoff\_upper\_of\_mgf}, Markov applied to $\exp(tX)$); symmetrically for $t\le0$, $\Pr[X\le k] \le \exp(\mu(e^t-1)-tk)$ (\texttt{avg\_chernoff\_lower\_of\_mgf}).
nodes.label: lem:chernoff

nodes.name: Closed-form tail bounds at the optimal $t$
nodes.statement: Plugging $t=\log(k/\mu)$ into Lemma~\ref{lem:chernoff}: for $k\ge\mu>0$, \[ \Pr[X\ge k] \;\le\; \exp\bigl(k-\mu-k\log(k/\mu)\bigr) \qquad(\mu=\E X), \] and symmetrically for $0<k\le\mu$, $\Pr[X\le k] \le \exp(k-\mu-k\log(k/\mu))$. Both closed forms are \emph{mean-scaled}: the exponent depends on the true $\mu$ directly, not on a crude worst-case range/variance proxy, which matters late in the saturation phase once few at-risk agents remain (Lemma~\ref{lem:stage2b}). The Lean statements are the generalized variants, which take only an \emph{upper} bound $\mu_{\mathrm{ub}}\ge\mu$ (\texttt{avg\_chernoff\_upper\_log}, used by the saturation phase) or a \emph{lower} bound $\mu_{\mathrm{lb}}\le\mu$ (\texttt{avg\_chernoff\_lower\_log}, used by the growth phase) on the true mean (the exact forms are the case of equality) --- monotonicity of the exponent in $\mu$ at the optimal $t$ makes both directions sound, and this is the form each phase actually needs, since the exact mean depends on $x=|I|/n$ while the phases only assume an inequality on $|I|$.
nodes.label: lem:chernofflog

nodes.name: Bias schedule
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{growthBias}(j) := \tfrac1{10}(\tfrac{11}{10})^j$, the deterministic bias target after $j$ growth rounds; monotone, $\le\tfrac14$ for $j\le9$, and $>\tfrac14$ at $j=10$.
nodes.label: def:growthbias

nodes.name: Single growth round
nodes.statement: Starting from opinion-$1$ fraction $\ge\tfrac12+\beta$ ($\tfrac1{10}\le\beta\le\tfrac14$), the probability of \emph{failing} to reach the next bias target (guaranteed growth factor $\tfrac{11}{10}$, comfortably below the true drift factor $\tfrac54$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:drift}) is at most $\exp(-n/10^7)$. Proved by computing a lower bound $\mu_{\mathrm{lb}} = n(\tfrac12+\tfrac54\beta)$ on the true mean via monotonicity of $p$ on $[\tfrac12+\beta,1]$ (an inline \texttt{nlinarith} computation, not a separate lemma), then applying the lower-tail bound \texttt{avg\_tail\_le\_log\_ge} at $k=n(\tfrac12+\tfrac{11}{10}\beta)$, and bounding the resulting exponent using Lemma~\ref{lem:logquad}.
nodes.label: lem:growthround

nodes.name: Union bound over growth rounds
nodes.statement: Starting from bias $\mathrm{growthBias}(i)$, after $j$ further rounds (with $i+j\le10$) the probability of failing to reach $\mathrm{growthBias}(i+j)$ is at most $j\exp(-n/10^7)$, by induction on $j$ via the $\mathrm{expList}$-conditioning idiom (mirroring the push protocol's \texttt{Main.lean}).
nodes.label: lem:growthfail

nodes.name: Phase 1
nodes.statement: Starting from opinion-$1$ fraction $\ge\tfrac35$, after $10$ rounds the opinion-$1$ fraction exceeds $\tfrac34$, except with probability $\le10\exp(-n/10^7)$.
nodes.label: lem:phase1

nodes.name: General per-round upper-tail bound
nodes.statement: Given a reference dissent bound $U_t\le M\le n/4$ and any target $k\ge\tfrac58M$ (an upper bound $\mu_{\mathrm{ub}}=\tfrac58M$ on the true one-round mean, via $1-p(x)=(1-x)^2(1+2x)\le\tfrac58(1-x)$ for $x\ge\tfrac34$), the probability the next dissent count exceeds $k$ is at most $\exp(k-\tfrac58M-k\log(k/(\tfrac58M)))$ (\texttt{saturation\_round\_closed}); the same conclusion holds for any directly-supplied upper bound $\mu_{\mathrm{ub}}$ on the true mean (\texttt{saturation\_round\_generic}, used by Stage 2b where the quadratic estimate below is the tight one).
nodes.label: lem:satclosed

nodes.name: Quadratic mean bound
nodes.statement: For any dissent bound $U_t\le M\le n$, the true one-round mean is at most $3M^2/n$ (the crude bound $1-p(x)\le3(1-x)^2$, dropping the $\tfrac58$ refinement). Used both by Stage 2b and by Stage 2c (at $M=10$).
nodes.label: lem:satquad

nodes.name: Numeric per-round bound
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:satclosed}'s exponent, simplified via Mathlib's quadratic-tight Pad\'e bound for $\log$ (\texttt{Real.le\_log\_one\_add\_of\_nonneg}) to the closed form $-\lambda^2/(k+\tfrac58M)$, $\lambda=k-\tfrac58M$.
nodes.label: lem:satnumeric

nodes.name: Stage 2a per-round contraction
nodes.statement: Guaranteed contraction factor $0.7$ (vs.\ the true $\tfrac58$): failure probability $\le\exp(-M/250)$.
nodes.label: lem:satcontract

nodes.name: Deterministic dissent target
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{satAfter}(n,M,i) := \max(500\log n,\ (0.7)^i M)$, the target dissent bound after $i$ Stage 2a rounds, clamped below at the floor $500\log n$; written in closed form (not recursively) so shifts by one round agree definitionally on the unclamped branch.
nodes.label: def:satafter

nodes.name: Stage 2a, union bound
nodes.statement: Starting from a dissent bound $M$ ($500\log n\le M\le n/4$), offset $i$ rounds in, the probability the dissent count exceeds $\mathrm{satAfter}(n,M,i+j)$ after $j$ further rounds is at most $j\,n^{-2}$, by induction on $j$ via the same $\mathrm{expList}$- conditioning idiom as Lemma~\ref{lem:growthfail}, with the tail direction flipped (dissent shrinking rather than opinion-$1$ count growing).
nodes.label: lem:satfail

nodes.name: Stage 2a, wrapped
nodes.statement: With $T_{2a}(n) := \ceil{6\log n}$: starting from any dissent bound $\le n/4$, after $T_{2a}(n)$ rounds the dissent count exceeds the floor $500\log n$ with probability at most $T_{2a}(n)\cdot n^{-2}$.
nodes.label: lem:stage2a

nodes.name: Stage 2b
nodes.statement: Provided $\log n\ge30$: whenever $U_t\le500\log n$, $\Pr[U_{t+1}>10] \le \exp(-\log n) = 1/n$. One round, jumping from the $\Theta(\log n)$ floor directly to the fixed constant $10$: since the mean is already tiny ($\Theta((\log n)^2/n)$), this single round has an astronomically small failure probability once $n$ is large enough to beat the relevant polynomial in $\log n$, which a degree-$11$ instance of Lemma~\ref{lem:exppow}, combined with the tighter tangent-line bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:loglog}, already secures at this modest threshold.
nodes.label: lem:stage2b

nodes.name: Stage 2c
nodes.statement: Whenever $U_t\le10$: $\Pr[U_{t+1}\ge1] \le 300/n$, via ordinary Markov applied to the nonnegative-integer $U_{t+1}$ ($\E[U_{t+1}]\le300/n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:satquad} at $M=10$) --- no concentration needed for the very last step.
nodes.label: lem:stage2c

nodes.name: Stages 2b+2c combined
nodes.statement: Two rounds, from $U_t\le500\log n$ to \emph{exactly} $U=0$, with total failure probability $\le\exp(-\log n)+300/n$, by chaining Lemma~\ref{lem:stage2b} then Lemma~\ref{lem:stage2c} via $\mathrm{expList}$-conditioning.
nodes.label: lem:sat2b2c

nodes.name: All three saturation stages combined
nodes.statement: $T_{2a}(n)+2$ rounds, from $U_t\le n/4$ to exactly $U=0$, with total failure probability $\le T_{2a}(n)\cdot n^{-2} + \exp(-\log n) + 300/n$.
nodes.label: lem:sat2a2b2c

nodes.name: Main failure bound, raw form
nodes.statement: For $\log n\ge30$ and $|I_0|\ge\tfrac35n$: over $10+(T_{2a}(n)+2)$ rounds, \[ \Pr[I_T\ne V] \;\le\; 10e^{-n/10^7} + \bigl(T_{2a}(n)\,n^{-2} + e^{-\log n} + 300/n\bigr), \] by gluing Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1} (growth) to Lemma~\ref{lem:sat2a2b2c} (saturation), exactly as the push protocol's \texttt{prNotAllInformed\_le} glues its own two phases.
nodes.label: lem:mainfail

nodes.name: Clean numeric bound
nodes.statement: Under the same hypotheses, the four error terms of Theorem~\ref{lem:mainfail} are each bounded by $O(1/n)$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:exppow} (to show $n$ dominates the relevant polynomials in $\log n$ once $\log n\ge30$), giving the single clean bound $\Pr[I_T\ne V] \le 500/n$.
nodes.label: lem:mainfailclean

nodes.name: 3-Majority and Voter with any number of colours
nodes.statement: In a round of 3-Majority every agent draws an ordered sample triple $(s_1,s_2,s_3)$ uniformly with replacement (Definition~\ref{def:round}); if $s_2$ and $s_3$ have the same colour it adopts that colour, otherwise the colour of $s_1$. In a round of Voter every agent adopts the colour of one uniformly random agent (itself included).
nodes.label: def:as-model

nodes.name: Two colours
nodes.statement: With colours $\{0,1\}$, a round of 3-Majority is the step of Definition~\ref{def:step}.
nodes.label: lem:as-bool

nodes.statement: Case analysis on the colours of the three samples.

nodes.name: Majorization, Schur-convex observables
nodes.statement: For $x,y\in\R^\Sigma$, $x\succeq y$ if $\sum x=\sum y$ and every sum of $y$ over a set $S\subseteq\Sigma$ is at most a sum of $x$ over a set of the same size (equivalently, for every $j$ the $j$ largest entries of $y$ sum to at most the $j$ largest entries of $x$). An observable $\varphi$ of configurations is Schur-convex if $(c_a)_a\succeq(c'_a)_a$ implies $\varphi(c')\le\varphi(c)$.
nodes.label: def:as-majorization

nodes.name: Majorization and colours
nodes.statement: If $(c_a)_a\succeq(c'_a)_a$ then $\kappa(c)\le\kappa(c')$. Hence the indicator of $\kappa(c)\le\kappa$ is Schur-convex.
nodes.label: lem:as-colours

nodes.statement: The colours of $c'$ carry all $n$ agents, so a set of $\kappa(c')$ colours carries all agents of $c$.

nodes.name: AC-processes and dominance, Definitions~1 and~2
nodes.statement: An anonymous consensus process with process function $\alpha$ moves from $c$ by letting every agent draw its new colour independently from the probability vector $\alpha(c)$. The process $\alpha$ dominates $\alpha'$ if $c\succeq c'$ implies $\alpha(c)\succeq\alpha'(c')$.
nodes.label: def:as-ac

nodes.name: Proposition~1, Rinott
nodes.statement: If $p\succeq q$ are probability vectors on $\Sigma$ and $\varphi$ is Schur-convex, the expectation of $\varphi$ when the $n$ agents draw their colours i.i.d.\ from $q$ is at most the expectation when they draw from $p$.
nodes.label: prop:as-rinott

nodes.statement: The paper cites this result without proof. For one Robin Hood transfer between colours $a$ and $b$, the expectation, as a function of the mass $\theta$ of $a$ (with $a$ and $b$ sharing a fixed total $s$), is nondecreasing on $[s/2,s]$: its derivative is a sum over agents, and swapping $a$ and $b$ for all agents and then for one agent pairs its terms into products of two factors with the same sign. A chain of transfers (the Hardy--Littlewood--P\'olya construction) leads from $p$ to $q$ when $q$ is sorted and the partial sums of $p$ dominate those of $q$; sorting and relabelling the colours, under which Schur-convex observables are invariant, reduce the general case to this one.

nodes.name: Theorem~2, distributional form
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ dominates $\alpha'$ and $c\succeq c'$, then for every Schur-convex $\varphi$ and every $T$, $\E_{c'}[\varphi(P'_T)]\le\E_c[\varphi(P_T)]$. In particular, from the same configuration, the dominating process has at most $\kappa$ colours at time $T$ with at least the probability of the dominated one.
nodes.label: thm:as-comparison

nodes.statement: Induction on $T$. With $u_T$, $v_T$ the expectations at time $T$ for the dominated and the dominating process, $w(y)=\max\{u_T(z):z\preceq y\}$ is Schur-convex and $u_T\le w\le v_T$ on comparable configurations, so Proposition~\ref{prop:as-rinott} applied to $w$ gives the step from $T$ to $T+1$. The second statement is the case of the indicator of Lemma~\ref{lem:as-colours}. The paper's coupling (Lemma~1, from Strassen's theorem) is not needed.

nodes.name: Equations~(1) and~(2)
nodes.statement: Both processes are AC-processes. With $x=c/n$, Voter has $\alpha^V_a(c)=x_a$ and 3-Majority has $\alpha^{3M}_a(c)=x_a(1+x_a-\|x\|_2^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:as-alpha

nodes.statement: The agents' samples are independent. For 3-Majority, $[\mathrm{maj}=a]=[x_2=a][x_3=a]+[x_1=a]-[x_2=x_3][x_1=a]$, and the number of pairs of agents of equal colour is $\sum_b c_b^2$.

nodes.name: Lemma~2
nodes.statement: 3-Majority dominates Voter. Hence, from the same configuration, after $T$ rounds 3-Majority has at most $\kappa$ colours with at least the probability that Voter has.
nodes.label: lem:as-vs-voter

nodes.statement: For a set $S$ of the largest entries of $x$, $\|x\|_2^2\sum_S x\le\sum_S x^2$, since $\sum_{i\in S}\sum_j x_ix_j(x_i-x_j)\ge0$; this gives $\alpha^{3M}(c)\succeq\alpha^V(c)$, and with $c\succeq c'$ also $\alpha^{3M}(c)\succeq\alpha^V(c')$. Conclude with Theorem~\ref{thm:as-comparison}.

nodes.name: Lemma~4 and Equation~(6), duality
nodes.statement: Let coalescing random walks start on all $n$ nodes of the complete graph with self-loops. After $T$ rounds, Voter has more than $k$ colours with at most the probability that more than $k$ walks remain.
nodes.label: lem:as-dual

nodes.statement: Pathwise, the colours of Voter after rounds $y_1,\dots,y_T$ are colours of the nodes occupied by the walks moved by $y_T,\dots,y_1$; the rounds are i.i.d., so reversing their order does not change the law. The paper proves an equality under a coupling and uses only this inequality.

nodes.name: Equation~(7) and the expected number of walks
nodes.statement: If $X_t$ walks remain, $\E[X_{t+1}\mid X_t=x]\le x-x(x-1)/(3n)$ for every $x$, hence $\le x-x^2/(10n)$ for $x\ge2$ (Equation~(7)). From any set of walks, $\E X_t\le1+3n/t$ for $t\ge1$.
nodes.label: lem:as-walks

nodes.statement: $\E[X_{t+1}\mid X_t=x]=n(1-(1-1/n)^x)$, the expected number of occupied cells when $x$ balls go into $n$ cells; bound $(1-1/n)^x$ by the Bonferroni inequality of degree~3. The map $x\mapsto x-x(x-1)/(3n)$ is concave and nondecreasing on $[0,n+1]$, so its tangent-line bound and induction on $t$ give $\E X_t\le1+3n/t$. This replaces the paper's variable drift argument for $\E[T^k_C]\le20n/k$.

nodes.name: Lemma~3
nodes.statement: For $n\ge2$, $k\ge1$ and $T\ge24(n/k)\log n$, from any configuration Voter has more than $k$ colours after $T$ rounds with probability at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: lem:as-voter-whp

nodes.statement: Blocks of $\lceil6n/k\rceil$ rounds: by Markov's inequality on $X-1$ (the walks never vanish), each block leaves more than $k$ walks with probability at most $1/2$, from any start. Restart over $\lfloor T/\lceil6n/k\rceil\rfloor\ge\log_2 n$ blocks (for $k<n$; for $k\ge n$ there is nothing to prove) and use Lemma~\ref{lem:as-dual}.

nodes.name: Phase~1
nodes.statement: For $n\ge2$, $k\ge1$ and $T\ge24(n/k)\log n$, from any configuration 3-Majority has more than $k$ colours after $T$ rounds with probability at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: lem:as-phase1

nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:as-vs-voter} and Lemma~\ref{lem:as-voter-whp}.

nodes.name: Phase~2: the cited result
nodes.statement: For $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathrm{Phase2}(\varepsilon)$ is the proposition (Theorem~3.1 of \cite{BCNPT16}, Theorem~8 of \cite{BCEKMN17}): there are $C,N$ such that for $n\ge N$, from any configuration with colours in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $k\le n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$ colours, 3-Majority has not reached consensus after any $T\ge C(k^2\sqrt{\log n}+k\log n)(k+\log n)$ rounds with probability at most $1/n$. This proposition is a hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:as-main}; Theorem~\ref{thm:mo-phase2} proves it for every $\varepsilon>0$ (Section~\ref{sec:bcnpt16-many-opinions}). The cited paper's ``w.h.p.''\ is $1-O(n^{-\lambda})$ for some $\lambda>0$, which gives the form $1/n$ by repeating the phase a constant number of times; the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mo-phase2} gives the form $1/n$ directly.
nodes.label: def:as-phase2

nodes.name: The asymptotics of Theorem~4
nodes.statement: For every $A\ge0$ there are $C,N$ such that for $n\ge N$ and $k=\lfloor n^{1/4}\log^{1/8}n\rfloor$: $n\ge2$, $1\le k\le n^{1/3-1/24}$, and $24(n/k)\log n+1+A(k^2\sqrt{\log n}+k\log n)(k+\log n)\le Cn^{3/4}\log^{7/8}n$.
nodes.label: lem:as-asymptotics

nodes.statement: From $\log y\le y^{1/4}$ and $\log^{1/8}y\le y^{1/24}$ for $y$ large.

nodes.name: Theorem~4 from Phase~2
nodes.statement: Assume $\mathrm{Phase2}(1/24)$. There are $C,N$ such that for $n\ge N$, from any configuration with colours in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, 3-Majority has not reached consensus after any $T\ge Cn^{3/4}\log^{7/8}n$ rounds with probability at most $2/n$.
nodes.label: thm:as-main

nodes.statement: Let $k=\lfloor n^{1/4}\log^{1/8}n\rfloor$ and $T_1=\lceil24(n/k)\log n\rceil$. After $T_1$ rounds, more than $k$ colours remain with probability at most $1/n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:as-phase1}); otherwise the current configuration has at most $k\le n^{1/3-1/24}$ colours, and $\mathrm{Phase2}(1/24)$ bounds the failure of the remaining $T-T_1$ rounds by $1/n$. Lemma~\ref{lem:as-asymptotics} fits both phases in $Cn^{3/4}\log^{7/8}n$ rounds. The proof in the paper needs a minor correction: it applies Lemma~3 with $k=n^{1/4}$, which gives $O(n^{3/4}\log n)$ rounds for Phase~1; the choice $k=n^{1/4}\log^{1/8}n$ balances the two phases and gives the bound as stated.

nodes.name: Theorem~4
nodes.statement: There are $C,N$ such that for $n\ge N$, from any configuration with colours in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, 3-Majority has not reached consensus after any $T\ge Cn^{3/4}\log^{7/8}n$ rounds with probability at most $2/n$.
nodes.label: thm:as-main-unconditional

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:as-main}, whose hypothesis $\mathrm{Phase2}(1/24)$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:mo-phase2} for $\varepsilon=1/24$.

nodes.name: Lemma~2.1
nodes.statement: For any finite set of colours, any configuration $c$ and any colour $a$, \[ \E[C'_a]=c_a\Bigl(1+\frac{c_a}{n}-\sum_b\frac{c_b^2}{n^2}\Bigr) \le c_a\Bigl(1+\frac{c_a}{n}-\frac{1}{\kappa(c)}\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:mo-expect

nodes.statement: $C'_a$ is the sum over the agents of independent indicators of adopting $a$, each with mean $x_a(1+x_a-\|x\|_2^2)$ for $x=c/n$ (as in Lemma~\ref{lem:as-alpha}). The inequality is the Cauchy--Schwarz bound $\sum_b c_b^2\ge n^2/\kappa(c)$.

nodes.name: One-round tails and anti-concentration
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_a^2$ be the sum of the variances of the agents' indicators of adopting $a$. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\E[C'_a]\le\mu<k$, then $\Pr(C'_a\ge k)\le\exp(-(k-\mu)^2/(k+\mu))$; if $0<k<\mu\le\E[C'_a]$, then $\Pr(C'_a\le k)\le\exp(-(\mu-k)^2/(2\mu))$. \item If $\sigma_a^2\ge1$, then $\E|C'_a-\theta|\ge(9/256)\,\sigma_a$ for every $\theta\in\R$. \item If $c$ has $j\ge2$ colours, all with more than $n/j-nu$ agents, where $u\ge0$ and $ju\le1/250$, then $\sigma_a^2\ge n/(4j)$ for every colour $a$ of $c$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:mo-tails

nodes.statement: (1) The Chernoff bounds of Section~\ref{sec:chernoff} for a sum of independent indicators. (2) If $|\E[C'_a]-\theta|\ge\sigma_a/4$, this is Jensen's inequality. Otherwise, by the Paley--Zygmund inequality (from the second and fourth moments of a sum of independent centred $\{0,1\}$-coordinates) the centred sum $S$ satisfies $\sigma_a^2\le4S^2$ with probability at least $9/64$, and there $|C'_a-\theta|\ge\sigma_a/2-\sigma_a/4$. (3) The adoption probability $p$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-expect} lies between $(1-1/250)^2/j$ and $(1/2+1/250)(1+1/250)$, and $\sigma_a^2=np(1-p)$.

nodes.name: Lemma~3.2, finite horizon
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a Markov kernel on a finite set, $I$ a set with $K(x,I)=1$ for $x\in I$, $B$ a target set with hitting time $\tau$, and $f$ a real function. Let $\beta,\eta\ge0$, and assume that $f(x)\le M$ for $x\in I$ and that, for $x\in I\setminus B$, $f(x)\le\beta$, $\E[f(X_1)\mid X_0=x]\ge f(x)+\lambda$ and $\Pr(f(X_1)>\beta\mid X_0=x)\le\eta$. Then for every $a\in I$ with $f(a)\ge0$ and every $t$, $\lambda t\Pr_a(\tau>t)\le\beta+M\eta t$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-drift

nodes.statement: Let $X'$ be the chain stopped at $B$. Summing the drift over the steps before $\tau$, $\E_a[f(X'_t)]\ge f(a)+\lambda\E_a[\min(t,\tau)]\ge\lambda t\Pr_a(\tau>t)$. By a union bound over the steps, $f(X'_t)>\beta$ with probability at most $\eta t$, and $f\le M$, so $\E_a[f(X'_t)]\le\beta+M\eta t$. The paper bounds $\E[\tau]$ by optional stopping, under a hypothesis on the overshoot at time $\tau$ (Lemma~B.1); the finite horizon and the one-step overshoot bound avoid both.

nodes.name: Hit, then absorb
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an absorbing set for $K$. If from every state of $B$ the chain is in $P$ after $s$ steps with probability at least $q$, then from every state $a$ it is in $P$ at time $t+s$ with probability at least $q\Pr_a(\tau\le t)$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-strong-markov

nodes.statement: The strong Markov property at $\tau$, proved by induction on $t$ without stopping times: from a state of $B$, the hypothesis and absorption; otherwise, condition on the first step.

nodes.name: Broken symmetry
nodes.statement: A configuration $x$ has broken symmetry for $j$ colours if $\kappa(x)<j$, or $\kappa(x)\le j$ and some colour has between $1$ and $n/j-16\sqrt{jn\log n}$ agents.
nodes.label: def:mo-broken

nodes.name: Equation~(3)
nodes.statement: There are $\delta>0$ and $C$ such that, for every configuration $x$ with $j=\kappa(x)\ge2$ colours, $Cj^3\log n\le n$ and every colour of $x$ above $n/j-m$ agents, the smallest support among the colours of $x$ (a colour that dies counting $0$) decreases in expectation by at least $\delta\sqrt n/(j\sqrt j)$ in one round.
nodes.label: lem:mo-min-drift

nodes.statement: Take $\delta=1/500$, $C=1024$ and $w=\sqrt{n/j}$. If the smallest support $c_{\min}$ is at most $n/j-w/250$, Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-expect} for a smallest colour, with $c_{\min}\ge n/(2j)$ (Equation~(5)), gives the drift. Otherwise all colours are above $n/j-w/250$. The supports sum to $n$, so the smallest new support is at most $n/j-\frac1{2j}\sum_a|C'_a-n/j|$, and $\E|C'_a-n/j|\ge(9/256)\sigma_a\ge(9/512)w$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-tails}; hence the expected smallest new support is at most $n/j-9w/1024<c_{\min}-w/1000$. The paper argues in this case with the Central Limit Theorem and negative association instead.

nodes.name: Equation~(6) and Lemma~B.1, one step
nodes.statement: There is $C$ such that, under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-min-drift}, one round puts some colour of $x$ below $n/j-64\sqrt{jn\log n}$ agents with probability at most $1/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-overshoot

nodes.statement: Take $C=2^{14}$. Every support is at most $n/j+(j-1)m$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-expect} every colour of $x$ has $\E[C'_a]\ge n/j-2m$. The Chernoff lower tail at $n/j-4m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-tails}) and a union bound over the at most $n$ colours give $1/n^2$. The paper bounds the overshoot at the hitting time instead (Lemma~B.1); its proof needs a minor correction, since it treats the smallest support as a Markov chain, while it is a function of the configuration. The one-step form avoids this argument.

nodes.name: Lemma~3.3, symmetry breaking
nodes.statement: There is $C$ such that, from every configuration $c$ with $j\ge2$ colours and $Cj^3\log n\le n$, 3-Majority reaches broken symmetry for $j$ colours within any $t\ge Cj^2\sqrt{\log n}$ rounds with probability at least $1/2$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-breaking

nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-drift} with $I=\{\kappa\le j\}$, $B$ the configurations with broken symmetry, $f=n/j$ minus the smallest support among the $j$ colours (the paper's $Y_t$), $\lambda=\delta\sqrt n/(j\sqrt j)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-min-drift}), $\beta=64\sqrt{jn\log n}$ and $\eta=1/n^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-overshoot}), and $M=n/j$. For $t\ge Cj^2\sqrt{\log n}$ (the proof takes $C=145\,409$), $\lambda t\ge4\beta$ and $M\eta t\le\lambda t/4$, so $\Pr(\tau>t)\le1/2$. The paper states the conclusion at the fixed time $t$, while its proof bounds the hitting time, which is what is stated here; its composition in Theorem~3.1 needs a minor correction, the strong Markov property at the hitting time (Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-strong-markov}). The statement also needs a minor correction: it needs the hypothesis $j^3\log n=O(n)$, as do the paper's Lemmas~3.4 and~3.5 (otherwise the threshold $n/j-\sqrt{jn\log n}$ is negative and the event has probability $0$). Finally, its bound $\E[\tau]<j^2\sqrt{\log n}$ should read $\E[\tau]\le(2\alpha/\varepsilon)j^2\sqrt{\log n}$.

nodes.name: Lemma~3.4, dropping stage~1
nodes.statement: There is $C$ such that, for $j\ge2$ with $Cj^3\log n\le n$, from every configuration with at most $j$ colours and every colour $a$ with at most $n/j-16\sqrt{jn\log n}$ agents, at every time $t$ with $Cj\log n\le t\le n$ colour $a$ has more than $Cj^2\log n$ agents with probability at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-stage1

nodes.statement: Take $C=240$. As in Appendix~B of the paper, the gap $n/j-c_a$ grows by a factor $1+1/(4j)$ per round until $c_a\le n/(2j)$, and then $c_a$ shrinks by a factor $1-1/(4j)$ per round down to a floor. Here both stages are one moving level, $\max\{n/j-m(1+1/(4j))^s,\ (n/(2j))(1-1/(4j))^{s-s_A},\ K\}$ at round $s$, with $K=\min\{240j^2\log n,n/(2j)\}$ and $s_A=\lceil5j\log n\rceil$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-expect} and the Chernoff upper tail (Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-tails}), $c_a$ exceeds the level of the next round with probability at most $1/n^2$; after $s_A+\lceil4j\log n\rceil\le240j\log n$ rounds the level is $K$, and a union bound over the $t\le n$ rounds gives $1/n$. The proof in the paper needs a minor correction. At its threshold $n/j-\sqrt{jn\log n}$, and again near its floor $j^2\log n$, the one-round bound of its Equation~(7) is only about $n^{-1/12}$, and the union bound over the rounds exceeds $1$ for large $j$ (for instance $j\ge20n^{1/10}$, which $j\le n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$ allows). The threshold $16\sqrt{jn\log n}$, which Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-breaking} reaches within the same $O(j^2\sqrt{\log n})$ rounds, and the floor $240j^2\log n$ make each round fail with probability at most $1/n^2$.

nodes.name: Lemma~3.5, dropping stage~2
nodes.statement: There is $C$ such that, for $j\ge2$ with $Cj^3\log n\le n$, from every configuration with at most $j$ colours and every colour $a$ with at most $n/(2j)$ agents, colour $a$ has died after any $t\ge Cj\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1/2$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-stage2

nodes.statement: Take $C=1024$. As in the paper's sketch, with the potential $\psi=\min\{c_a,n/(2j)\}$: Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-expect} gives $\E[\psi']\le(1-1/(2j))\psi+(n/(4j^2))[c_a>n/(2j)]$, and by the Chernoff upper tail $c_a$ escapes above $n/(2j)$ with probability at most $1/n^4$ per round. Hence $\E[\psi_s]\le(1-1/(2j))^s\,n/(2j)+(n/(4j^2))\,n^{-4}s^2$, which is at most $1/2$ at $s=\lceil2j\log n\rceil$, and Markov's inequality gives $\Pr(c_a\ge1)\le1/2$. Later times follow since a dead colour stays dead.

nodes.name: One phase
nodes.statement: There is $C$ such that, from every configuration with $j\ge2$ colours and $Cj^3\log n\le n$, after any $t\ge C(j^2\sqrt{\log n}+j\log n)$ rounds fewer than $j$ colours remain with probability at least $1/5$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-phase

nodes.statement: From a configuration with broken symmetry, either fewer than $j$ colours remain, or a colour has at most $n/j-16\sqrt{jn\log n}$ agents; then Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-stage1} brings it to at most $240j^2\log n\le n/(2j)$ agents except with probability $1/n$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-stage2} kills it with probability at least $1/2$: in total at least $\frac12(1-\frac1n)\ge\frac25$. Fewer than $j$ colours is absorbing, so Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-strong-markov} at the hitting time of broken symmetry and Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-breaking} give $\frac12\cdot\frac25=\frac15$ (the proof takes $C=293\,349$). The paper's proof of Theorem~3.1 needs a minor correction here: its probability $1/4$ ignores the failure probability of Lemma~3.4; any positive constant suffices.

nodes.name: Amplification over phases
nodes.statement: If from every configuration with between $2$ and $k$ colours a phase of $L$ rounds removes a colour with probability at least $p\le1$, then from every configuration with at most $k$ colours consensus fails after $M$ phases with probability at most $(1-p/2)^M2^k$.
nodes.label: lem:mo-phases

nodes.statement: The potential equal to $2^{\kappa}$ without consensus and to $0$ at consensus: colours never increase, and with probability at least $p$ one of them disappears, so over one phase its expectation is multiplied by at most $(1-p)+p/2=1-p/2$. This makes precise the paper's ``standard probabilistic arguments''.

nodes.name: Theorem~3.1, for $Ck^3\log n\le n$
nodes.statement: There is $C$ such that, from every configuration with $k$ colours and $Ck^3\log n\le n$, 3-Majority has not reached consensus after any $T\ge C(k^2\sqrt{\log n}+k\log n)(k+\log n)$ rounds with probability at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:mo-main

nodes.statement: Phases of $L=\lceil C_1(k^2\sqrt{\log n}+k\log n)\rceil$ rounds, with $C_1$ the constant of Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-phase}, which applies to every configuration with $2\le j\le k$ colours. By Lemma~\ref{lem:mo-phases} with $p=1/5$ and $M=10(k+\lceil\log n\rceil)$ phases, consensus fails after $ML$ rounds with probability at most $(9/10)^M2^k\le1/n$, and consensus is absorbing. The proof takes $C=15(C_1+1)=4\,400\,250$.

nodes.name: Theorem~3.1
nodes.statement: For every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathrm{Phase2}(\varepsilon)$ holds: there are $C,N$ such that for $n\ge N$, from every configuration with colours in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $k\le n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$ colours, 3-Majority has not reached consensus after any $T\ge C(k^2\sqrt{\log n}+k\log n)(k+\log n)$ rounds with probability at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:mo-phase2

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:mo-main} with the same $C$: $k^3\le n^{1-3\varepsilon}$ and $|C|\log n\le n^{3\varepsilon}$ for $n\ge N$, so $Ck^3\log n\le n$.

nodes.name: Averaging
nodes.statement: $x_{t+1}(v)=\frac1{\deg v}\sum_{u\sim v}x_t(u)$, and $\bar x=\sum_v\deg(v)\,x_0(v)/\sum_v\deg(v)$.
nodes.label: def:avg

nodes.name: Conservation and range
nodes.statement: $\sum_v\deg(v)\,x_{t}(v)$ does not depend on $t$; without isolated nodes, a round never leaves an interval containing all current values.
nodes.label: lem:basic

nodes.statement: Double counting over ordered adjacent pairs; an average of values in an interval stays in it.

nodes.name: Walk weights
nodes.statement: $x_t(v)=\sum_u W_t(v,u)\,x_0(u)$ with $W_t$ stochastic and $W_t(v,u)>0$ when a walk of length $t$ joins $v$ and $u$. On a connected graph with an odd closed walk, some length $L$ joins every pair.
nodes.label: lem:walks

nodes.statement: Induction on $t$; for $L$, fix the parity with the odd closed walk and pad with back-and-forth steps.

nodes.name: Convergence to the degree-weighted average
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk, $x_t(v)\to\bar x$ for every $v$.
nodes.label: thm:conv

nodes.statement: All entries of $W_L$ are at least some $\delta>0$, so $\max-\min$ contracts by $1-|V|\delta$ every $L$ rounds (Doeblin); the common limit is $\bar x$ by conservation.

nodes.name: Bipartite graphs
nodes.statement: On a connected bipartite graph with at least two nodes, the values $\pm1$ of a proper 2-colouring change sign at every round, so they converge nowhere.
nodes.label: thm:bip

nodes.statement: All neighbours of a node have the other colour.

nodes.name: Random walk and its spectrum
nodes.statement: $P=D^{-1}A$ is the transition matrix of the random walk, $N=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$ its symmetric version with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$, $\lambda=\max\{|\lambda_2|,|\lambda_n|\}$ ($0$ if $n<2$), and $\pi(v)=\deg(v)/2m$ with $m$ the number of edges.
nodes.label: def:walk

nodes.name: Matrix form of the dynamics
nodes.statement: $P^t(u,v)=W_t(u,v)$ is the probability that the walk from $u$ is at $v$ after $t$ steps, and $x_t=P^tx_0$. If every degree is positive, $P$ and $N$ have the same characteristic polynomial, so $\lambda$ is computed from the spectrum of $P$.
nodes.label: lem:walk-bridges

nodes.statement: Induction on $t$; $P=SNS^{-1}$ with $S=D^{-1/2}$.

nodes.name: Lovász's bound, Survey Theorem 33
nodes.statement: If every degree is positive, $|P^t(u,v)-\pi(v)|\le\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,\lambda^t$ for all nodes $u,v$ and all $t$.
nodes.label: thm:lovasz

nodes.statement: $P^t(u,v)=\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,N^t(u,v)$ and $\pi(v)=\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,s(u)s(v)$ with $s=\sqrt\pi$ a unit eigenvector of $N$ for the eigenvalue $1$. At most one eigenvalue of $N$ exceeds $\lambda$ in absolute value, and then it is $1$ with eigenvector $s$; so $N$ contracts $s^\perp$ by $\lambda$, and $N^t(u,v)-s(u)s(v)=\langle Qe_u,N^tQe_v\rangle$ with $Q=I-ss^\top$ is at most $\lambda^t$ by Cauchy--Schwarz.

nodes.name: Non-bipartite graphs
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with an odd closed walk, $\lambda<1$.
nodes.label: lem:lambda-lt-one

nodes.statement: An eigenvalue $\mu$ of $N$ with $|\mu|=1$ gives a vector $y$ with $x_t=\mu^ty$ for the dynamics started at $y$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:conv} $\mu=-1$ is impossible and $\mu=1$ forces $y$ constant, so $1$ is a simple eigenvalue and all others have absolute value below $1$.

nodes.name: Rate of the averaging dynamics
nodes.statement: If every degree is positive, $|x_t(u)-\sum_v\pi(v)x_0(v)|\le\lambda^t\sum_v\sqrt{\deg(v)/\deg(u)}\,|x_0(v)|$.
nodes.label: cor:avg-rate

nodes.statement: $x_t(u)-\sum_v\pi(v)x_0(v)=\sum_v(P^t(u,v)-\pi(v))x_0(v)$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:lovasz}.

nodes.name: Edge step
nodes.statement: A step on the edge $(i,j)$ multiplies the state by $W_{ij}=I-\frac12(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^\top$; a run applies the steps of a list of oriented edges in order. For a stochastic matrix $P$ (given as a kernel), $\bar W_P=I-\bar D/2n+(P+P^\top)/2n$ with $\bar D_{ii}=\sum_j(P_{ij}+P_{ji})$, and $\bar W=I-L/2m$ with $L$ the Laplacian.
nodes.label: def:edge-matrix

nodes.name: Properties of an edge step
nodes.statement: $W_{ij}x$ replaces $x_i$ and $x_j$ by their average and keeps the other values; $W_{ij}$ is doubly stochastic and a symmetric projection, $W_{ij}^\top W_{ij}=W_{ij}$.
nodes.label: lem:edge-matrix

nodes.statement: Direct computation; $(e_i-e_j)^\top(e_i-e_j)=2$ for $i\ne j$.

nodes.name: Expected step, Survey equations (4) and (5)
nodes.statement: If a uniformly random node $i$ contacts $j$ with probability $P_{ij}$, then $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W_P$; if a uniformly random oriented edge is selected, then $\mathbb E[W_{ij}]=\bar W$. On a $d$-regular graph with $d>0$ and $P=D^{-1}A$ both equal $(1-1/n)I+P/n$.
nodes.label: thm:mean-step

nodes.statement: Entrywise expansion of $W_{ij}(a,b)=\delta_{ab}-\frac12(\delta_{ia}-\delta_{ja})(\delta_{ib}-\delta_{jb})$; there are $\deg(a)$ darts out of $a$ and $2m=nd$ darts in all.

nodes.name: First and second moments
nodes.statement: For a uniformly random oriented edge, $\mathbb E[W^\top W]=\bar W$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$; after $t$ independent uniformly random oriented edges, $\mathbb E[x_t]=\bar W^tx_0$.
nodes.label: thm:moments

nodes.statement: $W^\top W=W$; for the first moment, induction on $t$ and linearity of expectation.

nodes.name: Clustered regular graph
nodes.statement: $G$ is $d$-regular on two clusters $V_1,V_2$ of $n$ nodes, each node having $b$ neighbours in the other cluster; $\chi=\mathbb 1_{V_1}-\mathbb 1_{V_2}$, $P=A/d$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots$, $\lambda=\max_{i\ge3}|\lambda_i|$. Node $v$ is blue at round $t$ if $x_t(v)\ge x_{t-1}(v)$; a coloring is a strong reconstruction if no color appears in both clusters. $T(n,\delta)=\lceil\log(4n^3)/\log(1+\delta)\rceil+1$.
nodes.label: def:clustered

nodes.name: Lemma C.1
nodes.statement: If $\lambda<1-2b/d$ and $x\in\{\pm1\}^{2n}$, then $|x_t(v)-\alpha_1-\alpha_2(1-2b/d)^t\chi(v)|\le\lambda^t\sqrt{2n}$ with $\alpha_1=\langle x,\mathbb 1\rangle/2n$, $\alpha_2=\langle x,\chi\rangle/2n$.
nodes.label: lem:c1

nodes.statement: $\mathbb 1$ and $\chi$ are eigenvectors with eigenvalues $1$ and $1-2b/d$, both above $\lambda$; at most two eigenvalues exceed $\lambda$ in absolute value, so by equality in Bessel's inequality their eigenvectors lie in $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbb 1,\chi\}$, and $P$ contracts the orthogonal complement of this plane by $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Deterministic core
nodes.statement: On a connected clustered graph with $1-2b/d>(1+\delta)\lambda$, if $x\in\{\pm1\}^{2n}$ and $\langle x,\chi\rangle\ne0$, then for $t\ge T(n,\delta)=O(\log n/\delta)$, $\operatorname{sgn}(x_{t-1}(u)-x_t(u))=\operatorname{sgn}(\langle x,\chi\rangle\chi(u))$.
nodes.label: thm:core

nodes.statement: $|\langle x,\chi\rangle|\ge2$ by parity, $b\ge1$ by connectivity, $d<2n$, and $(1+\delta)^{t-1}\ge4n^3$, so the main term of Lemma~\ref{lem:c1} dominates the errors.

nodes.name: Lemma B.1, exact form
nodes.statement: For uniform $x\in\{\pm1\}^{2n}$, $P(\langle x,\chi\rangle=0)=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\le1/\sqrt{\pi n}$.
nodes.label: lem:b1

nodes.statement: $x\mapsto\{v: x(v)=\chi(v)\}$ maps the zeros bijectively to the $n$-subsets; Wallis' product.

nodes.name: Strong reconstruction, Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement: With probability at least $1-1/\sqrt{\pi n}$, the coloring is a strong reconstruction at every round $t\ge T(n,\delta)$.
nodes.label: thm:strong

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:core} and Lemma~\ref{lem:b1}.

nodes.name: Opportunistic averaging, Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: One uniformly random edge is activated per round; a node activated for the first time draws a uniform sign, and both endpoints take the average of their two values. The rounds are i.i.d. uniform darts of $G$.
nodes.label: def:opp

nodes.name: Deferred decisions
nodes.statement: A uniform dart is a uniform edge; a node holds a value exactly when it has been activated, and the protocol's values are those of the averaging process started from the coins $\sigma$; the sum of the values is conserved.
nodes.label: lem:opp-model

nodes.statement: Induction on the list of rounds; every edge carries two darts.

nodes.name: Expected step, equations (1), (2), (15)
nodes.statement: $W_t$ is a symmetric projection, $\mathbb E[W]=\bar W=I-L/2m$ is symmetric and doubly stochastic, $\mathbb E[x^{(t)}]=\bar W^tx^{(0)}$ and $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$.
nodes.label: thm:opp-first

nodes.statement: Entrywise computation over the darts; induction on $t$.

nodes.name: Clustered regular graphs, Definition 2.2
nodes.statement: $G$ is $d$-regular with communities $V_1$ and $V_2=V_1^c$ of size $n/2$, each node having $b$ neighbours in the other community, $0<b$, $2b<d<n$. The state splits as $x=x_\parallel+y+z$ along $\mathbb 1$, $\chi=\mathbb 1_{V_1}-\mathbb 1_{V_2}$ and their orthogonal complement; $\lambda_2=2b/d$, and $\lambda_3$ enters as a lower bound on the Rayleigh quotient of $L/d$ on the complement.
nodes.label: def:opp-clustered

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1 on clustered regular graphs
nodes.statement: $\bar W\chi=(1-\lambda_2/n)\chi$, the expected state decomposes exactly as in Lemma B.1, and the monotonicity and sign criteria of Lemmas B.3 and B.4 hold at every node.
nodes.label: thm:opp-31

nodes.statement: $\bar W$ contracts the complement of $\operatorname{span}\{\mathbb 1,\chi\}$ by $1-\lambda_3/n$.

nodes.name: One round, Lemmas C.2 and C.3
nodes.statement: With $\beta=\langle x,\chi\rangle/n$: $\mathbb E\|z'\|^2\le(1-\lambda_3/n)\|z\|^2+\lambda_2\beta^2$ and, for every $\gamma$, $\mathbb E\,n(\beta'-\gamma)^2\le(1-\lambda_2/n)\,n(\beta-\gamma)^2+\lambda_2\gamma^2 +(4\lambda_2/n^2)(n\beta^2+\|z\|^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:opp-onestep

nodes.statement: $\mathbb E\|Wx\|^2=x^\top\bar Wx$ and Jensen for $\beta'$; the variance of $\beta'$ comes from the $nb$ darts across the cut.

nodes.name: Second moment analysis, Lemma C.4 and Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: If $100\lambda_2\log n\le\lambda_3$ and $3(n/\lambda_3)\log n\le t\le n/(4\lambda_2)$, then $\mathbb E\|y^{(t)}+z^{(t)}-y^{(0)}\|^2\le3\lambda_2t/n$.
nodes.label: thm:opp-41

nodes.statement: Unroll the two recursions from any state; average over the signs ($\mathbb E\|y^{(0)}\|^2=1$, $\|z^{(0)}\|^2\le n$).

nodes.name: Non-ephemeral good nodes, Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: If $\lambda_2/\lambda_3\le\lambda_3\varepsilon^4/(c\log^2n)$, then with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ at least $(1-3\varepsilon)n$ nodes are $\varepsilon$-good at every round of the phase $6(n/\lambda_3)\log n\le t\le12(n/\lambda_3)\log n$.
nodes.label: thm:opp-42

nodes.statement: Good nodes averaged only with good nodes of their community stay good; the bad rounds of the phase are counted in expectation from the second-moment bounds restarted at the start of the phase, and small initial cut components are handled by anti-concentration of $\langle\sigma,\chi\rangle$.

nodes.name: Sign recovery and weak reconstruction
nodes.statement: Under the hypothesis of Lemma 4.2, with probability at least $1-4\varepsilon$ at least $(1-4\varepsilon)n$ nodes have the sign of their community's initial average throughout the phase, and with probability at least $1/2-6\varepsilon$ the signs of the values are a $6\varepsilon$-weak reconstruction at every round of the phase.
nodes.label: thm:opp-main

nodes.statement: A good node has the sign of $2S_h/n$ unless $|S_1|\le\varepsilon|S_2|$ or $|S_2|\le\varepsilon|S_1|$ (each of probability at most $\varepsilon+1/\sqrt{n/2+1}$); $S_1S_2<0$ with probability at least $1/2-1/\sqrt{n/2+1}$.

nodes.name: Reactions, networks, counts
nodes.statement:
A reaction $A + B 	o C + D$ consumes the unordered pair $\{A, B\}$ of species and produces the unordered pair $\{C, D\}$; a network is a nonempty finite set of reactions whose products differ from their reactants. A count vector of $n$ molecules gives the number $x_a$ of molecules of each species $a$, with $\sum_a x_a = n$; firing an applicable reaction $r$ replaces $x_a$ by $x_a - 
u_a + 
u'_a$, with $
u$, $
u'$ the reactant and product multiplicities.
nodes.label: def:crn

nodes.name: Mass-action propensity
nodes.statement: With rate constant $k$, the propensity of $r$ at $x$ is $a_r(x) = k \prod_a \binom{x_a}{\nu_a}$ (Gillespie's combinatorial form), and $a_0(x) = \sum_r a_r(x)$.
nodes.label: def:propensity

nodes.name: Propensities
nodes.statement: For $A + B \to \cdots$ with $A \ne B$ the propensity is $k\, x_A x_B$; for $A + A \to \cdots$ it is $k \binom{x_A}{2}$.
nodes.label: lem:propensity

nodes.statement: Only the reactant species have nonzero multiplicity in the product.

nodes.name: Jump chain
nodes.statement: From $x$ with $a_0(x) > 0$ the jump chain fires $r$ with probability $a_r(x)/a_0(x)$; from a terminal state ($a_0(x) = 0$) it stays put.
nodes.label: def:jump

nodes.name: The jump chain jumps
nodes.statement: If $a_0(x) \ne 0$, the jump chain from $x$ gives weight $0$ to $x$.
nodes.label: lem:jump-self

nodes.statement: A reaction with nonzero propensity is applicable, and firing an applicable reaction whose products differ from its reactants changes the counts.

nodes.name: The population protocol of a network
nodes.statement: Each of $n \ge 2$ agents holds a species. One interaction draws a uniformly random ordered pair $(u, v)$ of distinct agents and, independently, a uniformly random reaction $r$ of the network; if the species of $u$ and $v$ are the reactants of $r$ the pair reacts and $r$ fires, otherwise nothing changes. The protocol is observed on count vectors; conditioning on the pair reacting gives a kernel on count vectors.
nodes.label: def:pp

nodes.name: Key identity
nodes.statement: The drawn pair has species $\{A, B\}$ with probability $x_A x_B / \binom{n}{2}$ if $A \ne B$, and $\binom{x_A}{2} / \binom{n}{2}$ if $A = B$. Equivalently, it has the reactants of $r$ with probability $a_r(x) / (k \binom{n}{2})$.
nodes.label: lem:pair

nodes.statement: There are $n(n-1)$ ordered pairs of distinct agents, $2 x_A x_B$ of them with species $\{A, B\}$ for $A \ne B$, and $x_A(x_A - 1)$ with species $\{A, A\}$.

nodes.name: One interaction
nodes.statement: The drawn pair reacts with probability $p = a_0(x) / (k\, |N| \binom{n}{2})$, and one interaction is a jump of the mass-action chain with probability $p$ and a no-op otherwise.
nodes.label: thm:step

nodes.statement: Average over the uniform reaction and apply the key identity to each reaction.

nodes.name: CRNs are population protocols
nodes.statement: For every rate constant $k > 0$ and $n \ge 2$, the population protocol conditioned on the drawn pair reacting is the jump chain of mass-action kinetics, from every configuration and hence as kernels on count vectors.
nodes.label: thm:crn1

nodes.statement: Conditioned on reacting, the interaction fires $r$ with probability proportional to $a_r(x)$ by the key identity, which is the jump chain; from a configuration where no pair can react both sides stay put.

nodes.name: The approximate-majority network
nodes.statement: Species $X$, $Y$ (the two opinions) and $B$ (blank), and the reactions $X + Y \to X + B$, $X + Y \to Y + B$, $B + X \to X + X$, $B + Y \to Y + Y$ (Angluin, Aspnes and Eisenstat).
nodes.label: def:am

nodes.name: Approximate majority as a population protocol
nodes.statement: With $D = 2 x_X x_Y + x_B (x_X + x_Y) > 0$, the jump chain fires each $X + Y$ reaction with probability $x_X x_Y / D$, $B + X \to X + X$ with probability $x_B x_X / D$ and $B + Y \to Y + Y$ with probability $x_B x_Y / D$; a drawn pair reacts with probability $D / (4 \binom{n}{2})$; and the jump chain is the population protocol conditioned on reacting.
nodes.label: thm:am

nodes.statement: Instances of the general results, with $a_0(x) = k D$.

nodes.name: Population protocols with input and output
nodes.statement: A population protocol has an input function $I : X \to Q$, an output function $O : Q \to \{0, 1\}$ and a transition function $\delta : Q \times Q \to Q \times Q$. An encounter of an ordered pair $(u, v)$ of distinct agents replaces their states $p, q$ by $\delta(p, q)$; reachability is the reflexive-transitive closure of encounters. A configuration is output-stable with output $b$ if in every configuration reachable from it every agent outputs $b$.
nodes.label: def:protocol

nodes.name: Stable computation
nodes.statement: A protocol stably computes a predicate $\varphi$ on input count vectors if, for every nonempty population and every input assignment $\iota$, every configuration reachable from $I \circ \iota$ can reach an output-stable configuration with output $\varphi$ of the input counts. A predicate is stably computable if a protocol with finitely many states stably computes it.
nodes.label: def:stable

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: A protocol stably computes at most one predicate on nonzero count vectors.
nodes.label: lem:stable-unique

nodes.statement: From the initial configuration of a population with the given counts, reach an output-stable configuration for the first predicate and then one for the second: they agree.

nodes.name: Boolean closure
nodes.statement: For every Boolean function $\xi$ of two arguments, if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are stably computable then so is $\xi(\varphi, \psi)$; in particular the class is closed under negation, conjunction and disjunction.
nodes.label: thm:boolean

nodes.statement: Parallel composition: states are pairs, both components make their own transition in every encounter, and the output of $(p_1, p_2)$ is $\xi(O_1 p_1, O_2 p_2)$.

nodes.name: Threshold predicates
nodes.statement: For integers $a_i$ and $c$, the predicates $\sum_i a_i x_i < c$ and $\sum_i a_i x_i \ge c$ are stably computable.
nodes.label: thm:threshold

nodes.statement: Each agent holds a leader bit, an output bit and a count in $[-s, s]$, starting from $a_i$; an encounter involving a leader merges the leaders into the initiator, which takes as much of the sum of the two counts as fits in $[-s, s]$, and both agents set their output to whether the initiator's count is below $c$. Unlike the original protocol, an input starts with output bit $[a_i < c]$, which is needed for a population of one agent. The second form is the negation.

nodes.name: Remainder predicates
nodes.statement: For integers $a_i$, $c$ and $m > 0$, the predicate $\sum_i a_i x_i \equiv c \pmod m$ is stably computable.
nodes.label: thm:remainder

nodes.statement: The same leader protocol with counts in $\mathbb{Z}/m$: the initiator takes the sum of the two counts and the responder gets $0$.

nodes.name: Semilinear predicates
nodes.statement: The Boolean combinations of threshold and remainder predicates.
nodes.label: def:semilinear

nodes.name: Semilinear predicates are stably computable
nodes.statement: The truth set of every such predicate is a semilinear set of count vectors, and every such predicate is stably computable.
nodes.label: thm:semilinear

nodes.statement: Induction on the Boolean combination, with the two preceding theorems and Boolean closure; for the first part, semilinear sets are closed under complement, intersection and union.

nodes.name: Stable decision by a network
nodes.statement: A network with an injective input map $I : X \to S$ and an output map $O : S \to \{0, 1\}$ stably decides $\varphi$ if, from the initial count vector with $x_i$ molecules of $I(i)$ and nothing else, every reachable count vector can reach one in which, now and in every count vector reachable from it, every present species votes $\varphi(x)$.
nodes.label: def:crn-stable

nodes.name: Protocols are networks
nodes.statement: The transitions $p + q \to \delta_1(p, q) + \delta_2(p, q)$ that change $\{p, q\}$ form a count-conserving bimolecular network whose reachable count vectors are the counts of the configurations reachable in the protocol. Hence every stably computable predicate, and in particular every Boolean combination of threshold and remainder predicates, is stably decided by such a network.
nodes.label: thm:transfer

nodes.statement: Encounters change counts exactly by the corresponding reaction. Tagging the input states keeps the input map injective and provides a transition that changes the multiset of states.

nodes.name: Protocols on an interaction graph
nodes.statement: On a graph $G$ on the agents, an encounter is an oriented edge $(u, v)$ of $G$ (initiator $u$, responder $v$). Reachability and output stability on $G$ are defined as before with encounters along edges of $G$. A protocol stably computes $\varphi$ on $G$ for inputs in a domain $D$ if, for every input whose count vector lies in $D$, every configuration reachable on $G$ can reach an output-stable configuration with output $\varphi$; it stably computes $\varphi$ on graphs if it does so on every connected graph.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:graph-stable

nodes.name: The complete graph
nodes.statement: On the complete graph these notions are those of Definition~\ref{def:stable}: stable computation on the complete graphs of all nonempty populations, with the trivial domain, is stable computation.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: lem:graph-top

nodes.statement: Every ordered pair of distinct agents is an oriented edge of the complete graph.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: Embedding a population
nodes.statement: Reachability transfers along an injective map of agents that preserves edges, the other agents being frozen.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: lem:graph-extend

nodes.statement: Induction on reachability: an encounter along $(u, v)$ is simulated along $(f(u), f(v))$.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: Majority
nodes.statement: With two input types, red and green, majority is true if red has more agents than green, and the domain excludes ties.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:majority

nodes.name: The ambassador protocol
nodes.statement: A state is a color and a bit saying whether the vertex holds an ambassador; every agent starts with an ambassador of its input color, and the output is the color. Two ambassadors of different colors annihilate; an ambassador meeting a vertex without ambassador moves there and paints it; nothing else changes. This is the table of Figure~1, with $4$ states, and the protocol is symmetric.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:ambassador

nodes.name: Invariants
nodes.statement: The number of ambassadors of each color starts at the input count and never increases, and the difference between red and green ambassadors never changes.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: lem:amb-invariant

nodes.statement: Count the two agents of an encounter, over the $16$ entries of the table.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: Annihilation and spreading
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, while both colors have ambassadors, a configuration with one ambassador of each color fewer is reachable. If all ambassadors have color $b$ and there is one, the all-$b$ coloring is reachable, and it is output-stable.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: lem:amb-steps

nodes.statement: Take a red ambassador and a closest green one. The red ambassador walks along a shortest path, moving onto vertices without ambassador and handing over to red ambassadors it meets, until it meets the green one (strong induction on the distance). Spreading is similar, by induction on the distance to a vertex of the other color and then on the number of such vertices.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 2
nodes.statement: The ambassador protocol stably computes majority on every connected graph, for every input with a majority. With one red and one green agent, a configuration is reachable from which no output-stable configuration is reachable, so ties must be excluded.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: thm:ambassador

nodes.statement: From every reachable configuration, annihilate pairs until only ambassadors of the majority color remain (there is one by the invariant), then spread that color. Configurations without ambassadors are frozen.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 1
nodes.statement: No protocol with at most $3$ states stably computes majority, ties excluded, on the complete graphs of all nonempty populations, hence on all connected graphs. With Theorem~\ref{thm:ambassador}, $4$ is the minimal number of states.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: thm:three-states

nodes.statement: A single agent never interacts, so both outputs occur, and one output $b$ has a single state $q_1$. On $3$ agents, the inputs $(b, b, \lnot b)$ and $(b, b, b)$ both reach the configuration in which every agent is in $q_1$. Adding two agents of input $\lnot b$ and running the same encounters on the first three agents, inputs with majority $\lnot b$ and $b$ reach a common configuration, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: Approximate majority on a graph
nodes.statement: The one-way rule: the initiator never changes; an initiator $X$ or $Y$ turns an opposite responder blank and recruits a blank responder. Its effective transitions are exactly the reactions of the approximate-majority network. Each step activates a uniformly random oriented edge of $G$.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:am-graph

nodes.name: Winning probabilities
nodes.statement: With $m$ agents of type $Y$ placed on a uniformly random $m$-set and $X$ elsewhere, $\mathrm{win}_t(s)$ is the probability that every agent is $s$ at time $t$. Unanimity is absorbing, so $\mathrm{win}_t(s)$ is nondecreasing in $t$, and its supremum, the convergence probability, is its limit.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: def:winprob

nodes.name: Coupling and symmetry
nodes.statement: For the order $Y < B < X$ the rule is monotone in both states, so the probability that every agent is $X$ at time $t$ is monotone in the initial configuration. Exchanging $X$ and $Y$ commutes with the dynamics.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: lem:am-coupling

nodes.statement: Run two ordered configurations with the same oriented edges; they stay ordered.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: MNRS14, Corollary 1
nodes.statement: A family of $r$-element subsets of a finite universe, with at most as many sets as elements, in which every element lies in the same number $d \ge 1$ of sets, has a system of distinct representatives. In particular, if $n \le 2m$, every $m$-set $S$ of agents contains an $(n - m)$-subset $A_S$, with $S \mapsto A_S$ injective on the $m$-sets.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: lem:hall

nodes.statement: Hall's theorem, with Hall's condition by double counting.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 4, at every finite time
nodes.statement: On every graph with an edge, if $n \le 2m$, at every time $t$ the probability that the minority $X$ has won is at most the probability that the majority $Y$ has won; hence the same holds for the convergence probabilities.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: thm:am-graph

nodes.statement: For each $m$-set $S$, the configuration with $X$ exactly on $A_S$ lies below the one with $X$ exactly on $S$, which is the swap of the placement with $Y$ on $S$. By monotonicity and symmetry, the minority wins from the first with probability at most the probability that the majority wins from the placement on $S$. The first configuration is the placement on the $m$-set $A_S^c$, and $S \mapsto A_S^c$ is a bijection of the $m$-sets, so averaging over $S$ gives the inequality (eqs.~(18) to~(23)).
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: MNRS14, Theorem 4
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, from every configuration with a non-blank agent, the protocol is absorbed in all-$X$ or all-$Y$ with probability tending to $1$. Hence, if $n \le 2m$ and $m \le n$, it converges to the majority with probability at least $1/2$.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)
nodes.label: thm:am-half

nodes.statement: An initiator $s \ne B$ activated twice on the same responder makes it $s$, so an opinion present spreads to all agents along the edges of a connected graph, and all-blank is never reached. Absorption in a finite chain follows, and the two convergence probabilities sum to $1$.
nodes.section: 24 Majority on graphs with very small local memory (CRN-4)

nodes.name: Stable computation with general outputs
nodes.statement: For an output map $O : Q \to Y$ into any type and a target $g(x, i) \in Y$ depending on the input counts $x$ and on an agent's input $i$, a protocol stably marks the agents with $g$ if, for every nonempty population, every configuration reachable from the initial one can reach a configuration from which every agent $v$ forever outputs $g(x, \iota(v))$. Stable computation of $f$ is the case $g(x, i) = f(x)$; with the protocol's Boolean output it is Definition~\ref{def:stable}.
nodes.label: def:em-marks

nodes.name: The static protocol
nodes.statement: Colours are in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. The six states are the strong states $[x]$ and the weak states $\langle x \rangle$, $x \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$, of weight $x$ and $0$. The states $[1]$ and $[-1]$ annihilate into $[0], [0]$; a strong $[x]$ turns a weak state into $\langle x \rangle$, and, for $x \ne 0$, turns $[0]$ into $\langle x \rangle$. The output of $[x]$ and $\langle x \rangle$ is $x$.
nodes.label: def:em-static

nodes.name: Lemmas 1 and 2
nodes.statement: Along every execution the weight sum equals the colour sum $S$, the sum $R$ of the absolute weights does not increase, and a configuration with $R = |S|$ is reachable.
nodes.label: lem:em-static

nodes.statement: Check the encounters (by computation over the $36$ pairs); while weights of both signs are present, bring two of them together, which decreases $R$.

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Theorem 3
nodes.statement: The static protocol stably computes $\operatorname{sign}(\#1 - \#(-1))$: all agents eventually and forever output $1$, $-1$, or $0$ for a tie.
nodes.label: thm:em-static

nodes.statement: Once $R = |S|$, every weight is $0$ or $s = \operatorname{sign} S$ and a strong agent $[s]$ exists (for $s = 0$, a strong state is never lost). It recruits every agent into the states of output $s$, a set closed under the transitions.

nodes.name: The dynamic protocol
nodes.statement: The eight states are the strong states $[-2], \dots, [2]$ and the weak states $\langle -1 \rangle, \langle 0 \rangle, \langle 1 \rangle$. Opposite strong states cancel as far as possible, and strong states recruit weak ones and $[0]$ as in the static protocol; the transitions do not read the colours. When an external force changes a colour $c$ to $c'$, the state becomes $[w + c' - c]$, $w$ its weight. For Section~5 the protocol runs separately in groups of agents, with encounters inside a group.
nodes.label: def:em-dynamic

nodes.name: Invariants of Section~3
nodes.statement: In every group the colour sum equals the weight sum, every agent's weight is within $1$ of its colour, and every group contains a strong state. The initial configuration $[c_a]$ satisfies them.
nodes.label: def:em-dyninv

nodes.name: Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement: The invariants are preserved by encounters inside groups and by colour changes. The sum of the absolute weights does not increase, and a configuration without opposite weights in a group is reachable.
nodes.label: lem:em-dynamic

nodes.statement: Encounter by encounter (by computation over the finite state space); a colour change moves the weight by the change of colour and makes the state strong.

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Section 3
nodes.statement: From every configuration satisfying the invariants, a configuration is reachable from which every agent forever outputs the sign of the colour sum of its group. Hence after any finite interleaving of encounters and colour changes the dynamic protocol stabilizes on the sign of the final colour sum, and without the force it stably computes $\operatorname{sign}(\#1 - \#(-1))$.
nodes.label: thm:em-dynamic

nodes.statement: After Lemma~5, every nonzero weight in a group has the sign $s$ of the group's colour sum, and a strong agent of weight sign $s$ exists in the group (the third invariant gives it in the tie case). It recruits the group into the states of output $s$.

nodes.name: Driving the dynamic protocol
nodes.statement: Given a protocol $D$, a colour map from its states to $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ and a group map that $D$ never changes, the driven protocol runs $D$ and a copy of the dynamic protocol: in an encounter $D$ makes its transition, the dynamic protocol makes its transition if the two agents are in the same group, and each agent whose colour changed applies the state change of the force.
nodes.label: def:em-drive

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.statement: Along every execution of the driven protocol the invariants of Section~3 hold for the derived colours. If $D$ stably marks the agents with their eventual colours, the driven protocol stably marks every agent with the sign of the eventual colour sum of its group.
nodes.label: thm:em-drive

nodes.statement: An encounter is an encounter of the dynamic protocol inside a group followed by two colour changes. Once $D$ has stabilized, the colours are fixed and Theorem~\ref{thm:em-dynamic} applies in every group.

nodes.name: Absolute-Majority
nodes.statement: Every agent keeps its label $l$ and runs $k$ copies of the static protocol on the bits $l[i]$, read as $\pm 1$. They drive a copy of the dynamic protocol, with colour $1$ if every copy currently reports the agent's own bit and $-1$ otherwise. An agent outputs the reported majority bits if its dynamic protocol outputs $1$, and none otherwise. The specification is the colour held by more than half of the agents, if any.
nodes.label: def:em-absolute

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Theorem 6
nodes.statement: Absolute-Majority stably computes the absolute majority colour, or reports that there is none, with $2^k \cdot 6^k \cdot 8 \le 2^{4k+3}$ states.
nodes.label: thm:em-absolute

nodes.statement: The $k$ copies stabilize on the majority bits one at a time. Then the colour of an agent is $1$ exactly when its label consists of the majority bits, so the eventual colour sum is positive if and only if that label is held by more than half of the agents, and the composition theorem applies with a single group.

nodes.name: Relative-Majority
nodes.statement: Stages $i = k - 1, \dots, 0$: the agents whose labels share the prefix $l[0..i-1]$ form a group, and a copy of the dynamic protocol runs in each group, with colour $l[i]$ (as $\pm 1$) for the agents that won all the stages above $i$ and $0$ for the others. An agent wins stage $i$ if its colour is $-1$ and the stage outputs $-1$, or its colour is $1$ and the stage outputs $0$ or $1$. The protocol is the $k$-fold iteration of the driven protocol, the colours being derived from the states. The plurality colour is the most frequent one, ties broken in favour of the lexicographically largest label.
nodes.label: def:em-relative

nodes.name: The duel
nodes.statement: Once the stages above $i$ have stabilized, the duel of stage $i$ between the winners of the two groups extending a prefix $p$ selects the winner of the group of $p$. The winner of the whole population is the plurality colour.
nodes.label: lem:em-duel

nodes.statement: The colour sum of the group of $p$ is the difference of the counts of the two group winners, and ties go to the larger label.

nodes.name: GHMSS16, Theorem 7
nodes.statement: Relative-Majority stably marks the agents of the plurality colour: eventually and forever, every agent outputs whether its own colour is the plurality colour. It has $2^k \cdot 8^k = 2^{4k}$ states.
nodes.label: thm:em-relative

nodes.statement: Induction on the levels: level $m$ stably marks every agent with whether its label wins its group of prefix length $k - m$, by the composition theorem and the duel lemma.

nodes.name: Finite uniform average
nodes.statement: For a finite type $A$, set $\operatorname{avg}(f)=\sum_{a\in A}f(a)/|A|$. When $A$ is empty this is zero, following Lean's division convention.
nodes.label: def:avg

nodes.name: Product independence
nodes.statement: Uniform averages factor over independent coordinates and are invariant under bijections of the sample space.
nodes.label: lem:uniform-product

nodes.name: Finite trajectories
nodes.statement: The recursively defined expectation over $T$ independent draws equals the uniform average over functions $\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\to A$.
nodes.label: lem:uniform-trajectory

nodes.statement: Separate the first coordinate using the finite-function/product equivalence, then induct on $T$. The empty sample space is handled separately.

nodes.name: Averages commute
nodes.statement: Iterated uniform averages over two finite sets commute; in particular an outer average commutes with the trajectory expectation $\mathrm{expList}$, which also commutes with finite sums and vanishes on the zero functional.
nodes.label: lem:avg-commute

nodes.statement: Exchange the order of finite summation; for $\mathrm{expList}$, induct on $T$.

nodes.name: Normalized real weights
nodes.statement: A distribution consists of nonnegative real weights $p_a$ with $\sum_a p_a=1$. Its expectation is $\sum_a p_a f(a)$, and an event probability is the expectation of its indicator. Such a distribution cannot exist on an empty type.
nodes.label: def:distribution

nodes.name: Uniform agreement
nodes.statement: On a nonempty finite type the normalized uniform distribution agrees with the existing finite average.
nodes.label: lem:uniform-agreement

nodes.name: Independent products and pushforward
