nodes.statement: There are constants $z,C>0$ such that, whenever $\log n\ge C$: if colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $z\sqrt{n\log n}$, then after $\lceil C(n/c_i)\log n\rceil$ rounds it holds at least $3n/4$ nodes with probability at least $1-C/n$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-growth-phase

nodes.statement: Take $z=C=128$, $a_0=c_i$, $g_0$ the initial lead and $q=1+a_0/(8n)$. Consider the moving targets ``colour $i$ holds $3n/4$ nodes, or it holds at least $a_0$ nodes and leads every other colour by $g_0q^t$''. Each round leaves them with probability at most $2/n^2$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-round} while $a\le3n/4$, and because a colour holding $3n/4$ nodes keeps them except with probability $n^{-2}$ (Bernstein, drift from the aggregation bound). Since $q^{\lceil128(n/a_0)\log n\rceil}>n$, a lead of $g_0q^t$ is impossible at the end, so the colour holds $3n/4$ nodes.

nodes.name: Finishing phase
nodes.statement: If $\log n\ge128$ and colour $i$ holds at least $3n/4$ nodes, all nodes hold $i$ after $\lceil128\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-128/n$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-finish

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}, colour $i$ dominates the binary median process started from its indicator, whose gap is at least $n/2\ge128\sqrt{n\log n}$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:whp}.

nodes.name: Plurality consensus, Theorem~1.2 without the adversary
nodes.statement: There are constants $z,C>0$ such that, whenever $\log n\ge C$, for every number $k$ of colours: if colour $i$ leads every other colour by at least $z\sqrt{n\log n}$, all nodes hold $i$ after $\lceil C(n/c_i)\log n\rceil$ rounds, and hence after $\lceil Ck\log n\rceil$ rounds, with probability at least $1-C/n$.
nodes.label: thm:tc-plurality

nodes.statement: Take $z=128$ and $C=384$: Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-phase}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-finish} from the configuration reached, with failure at most $256/n$; consensus is absorbing, so more rounds do not hurt. For the second form, $c_i\ge n/k$. The paper's proof of Theorem~1.2 needs a minor correction (the range $n/2<a<(1/2+\varepsilon_1)n$ and the time bound), which Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-growth-round} supplies.

nodes.name: Two colours and almost-sure consensus
nodes.statement: With two colours, a gap of $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ gives consensus on the majority after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-C/n$, whenever $\log n\ge C$. With finitely many colours, consensus is reached almost surely.
nodes.label: thm:tc-two

nodes.statement: On two colours the process is the binary median process (Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}); apply Theorem~\ref{thm:whp}. The round in which every node samples node $0$ twice gives consensus and has positive probability; conclude with the shared absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Few nodes change colour
nodes.statement: The number of nodes that see colour $i$ twice is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli variables of parameter $(c_i/n)^2$, so $\E e^{\theta\,\mathrm{twice}_i}=(1+(c_i/n)^2(e^\theta-1))^n$. The expected number of nodes whose two samples hold different colours is $n-S/n$, and if every colour has at most $\ell$ nodes, the expected number of nodes that change colour is at most $\ell$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-few-changes

nodes.statement: The samples of different nodes are independent. Two samples hold the same colour with probability $S/n^2$, and only such nodes can change colour; $S\le\ell n$.

nodes.name: One colour does not grow fast
nodes.statement: If $c_i\le L$, then for every $T$, the probability that $c_i(t)>L$ for some $t\le T$ is at most $\exp(-(L-c_i)+(e-1)TL^2/n)$.
nodes.label: lem:tc-escape

nodes.statement: Induction on the horizon. While $c_i\le L$, $c_i'\le c_i+\mathrm{twice}_i$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-basic}) and, with $\theta=1$, $\E e^{\mathrm{twice}_i}\le\exp((e-1)n(c_i/n)^2)\le\exp((e-1)L^2/n)$, so $e^{c_i(t)-(e-1)tL^2/n}$, stopped when $c_i$ exceeds $L$, is a supermartingale; conclude with Markov's inequality. This replaces the paper's domination by a process with binomial increments.

nodes.name: Theorem~5
nodes.statement: There is a constant $\gamma_0$ such that for every $\gamma\ge\gamma_0$: if every colour has at most $\ell$ nodes, $\ell'=\max\{2\ell,\gamma\log n\}$ and $T<n/(\gamma\ell')$, the probability that some colour has more than $\ell'$ nodes at some time $t\le T$ is at most $1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:tc-lower-strong

nodes.statement: Take $\gamma_0=8$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tc-escape} with $L=\ell'$, since $L-c_i\ge\ell'/2$ and $T\ell'^2/n<\ell'/\gamma$, one colour exceeds $\ell'$ with probability at most $\exp(-\ell'(1/2-(e-1)/\gamma))\le n^{-2}$; take a union bound over the at most $n$ colours present. A constant in the paper's proof needs a minor correction ($\gamma\ge36$ instead of $\gamma\ge18$ in its Chernoff step); the theorem is unaffected.

nodes.name: 2-Choices needs $\Omega(n/\log n)$ rounds, Theorem~1 (Simplified)
nodes.statement: For every $\beta>0$ there is $C>0$ such that, from every configuration in which every colour has at most $\beta\log n$ nodes, 2-Choices reaches consensus at some time $t\le T$ with probability at most $1/n$, for every $T$ with $(T+1)C\log n<n$.
nodes.label: thm:tc-lower

nodes.statement: Take $\gamma=\max\{8,2\beta\}$ and $C=\gamma^2$. Then $\ell'=\gamma\log n$, the window of Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-lower-strong} contains $T$, and consensus would put $n>\ell'$ nodes on one colour.

nodes.name: Birth--death Moran kernel
nodes.statement: Mutants have fitness $r>0$ and residents fitness $1$. A step chooses a parent $u$ with probability proportional to its fitness and an offspring position $w$ uniformly among the neighbours of $u$ (or $w=u$ if $u$ is isolated); the individual at $w$ is replaced by a copy of the parent.
nodes.label: def:moran

nodes.name: The kernel is well defined
nodes.statement: The weights of (parent, offspring position) pairs are nonnegative and sum to one.
nodes.label: lem:well-defined

nodes.statement: Sum over the offspring position first: each parent's placement weights sum to one. The remaining sum of fitnesses over the total fitness is one.

nodes.name: Birth mass is $r$ times death mass
nodes.statement: On a $d$-regular graph, the probability that a step adds a mutant equals $r$ times the probability that it removes one: both are proportional to the number of edges between the two types, counted from either side.
nodes.label: lem:birth-death

nodes.statement: For $d>0$ both masses are the oriented cut divided by $Fd$, weighted by the parent's fitness; the cut is symmetric under swapping endpoints. For $d=0$ both masses vanish.

nodes.name: Invariant potentials
nodes.statement: On a regular graph, $(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}}$ is preserved in expectation by one step; when $r=1$, so is the number of mutants.
nodes.label: thm:invariance

nodes.statement: A step changes the number of mutants by $\pm1$ or not at all, so its expectation is affine in the birth and death masses, and these cancel by the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Fixation or extinction
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, the probability that neither type has taken over tends to zero.
nodes.label: thm:absorption

nodes.statement: Constant configurations are absorbing. From a mixed configuration, a mutant adjacent to a resident (which exists by connectivity) reproduces onto it with positive probability; by induction on the number of residents, fixation is reachable. Apply the shared finite-chain absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Fixation from an invariant
nodes.statement: Let an observable be invariant in expectation, equal to $1$ on the all-mutant and to $0$ on the all-resident configuration. If the all-mutant configuration is absorbing and the probability that neither type has taken over tends to zero, the observable is the fixation probability.
nodes.label: lem:fixation-limit

nodes.statement: This is the finite-horizon optional stopping theorem of the shared \texttt{dynamics} package (\texttt{Dynamics.Kernel.iSup\_event\_of\_invariant}, roadmap FND-4) with the two constant configurations as targets: the fixation and unfixed indicators are the corresponding events.

nodes.name: Isothermal theorem
nodes.statement: On a connected regular graph with $r\neq1$, the fixation probability from $k$ mutants is $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$.
nodes.label: thm:isothermal

nodes.statement: Apply the previous lemma to $\psi=(1-(1/r)^{\#\text{mutants}})/(1-(1/r)^n)$, invariant by the invariance theorem and equal to $1$ and $0$ on the two constant configurations; the absorption theorem gives the vanishing survival probability.

nodes.name: Neutral case
nodes.statement: On a connected regular graph with $r=1$, the fixation probability is $k/n$.
nodes.label: thm:neutral

nodes.statement: The same argument with $\psi=\#\text{mutants}/n$.

nodes.name: Moran's formula
nodes.statement: On the complete graph, the fixation probability from $k$ mutants is $(1-r^{-k})/(1-r^{-n})$.
nodes.label: thm:moran

nodes.statement: The complete graph is connected and $(n-1)$-regular.

nodes.name: Death--Birth kernel
nodes.statement: In one pull (death--Birth) step, a uniformly random vertex $u$ adopts the type of a uniformly random neighbour $w$ (an isolated vertex keeps its type), so the pair $(u,w)$ has weight $\frac1n\cdot\frac1{\deg u}$ for $w\sim u$. The neutral push (Birth--death) process is the Moran kernel with $r=1$.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: def:pull

nodes.name: Reproductive values
nodes.statement: For a configuration with mutant set $S$, $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}1/\deg v$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}\deg v$.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: def:repro

nodes.name: Reproductive values are invariant
nodes.statement: On every finite graph, $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}$ is invariant in expectation under neutral push and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}$ is invariant in expectation under pull.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: thm:pushpull-invariance

nodes.statement: Write $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ for the type of $v$. Under push, the pair (parent $u$, target $w\sim u$) has weight $\frac1n\frac1{\deg u}$ and changes $\Phi_{\mathrm{push}}$ by $(x_u-x_w)/\deg w$, so the expected change is $\frac1n\sum_{u\sim w}(x_u-x_w)/(\deg u\deg w)$. Under pull, $u$ copies $w\sim u$ with weight $\frac1n\frac1{\deg u}$ and changes $\Phi_{\mathrm{pull}}$ by $(x_w-x_u)\deg u$, so the expected change is $\frac1n\sum_{u\sim w}(x_w-x_u)$. Both sums are over ordered adjacent pairs of an antisymmetric function, hence vanish.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Fixation or extinction under pull
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, the probability that the pull process has not reached a constant configuration after $t$ steps tends to $0$.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: thm:pull-absorption

nodes.statement: As for push: constant configurations are absorbing, and from any other configuration a resident adjacent to a mutant copies it with positive probability, so the number of mutants reaches $n$ with positive probability; the shared absorption theorem concludes.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Push and pull fixation
nodes.statement: On a connected graph with at least two vertices, the fixation probability of a mutant set $S$ is $\sum_{v\in S}\frac1{\deg v}\big/\sum_{v\in V}\frac1{\deg v}$ under neutral push and $\sum_{v\in S}\deg v/(2|E|)$ under pull.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs
nodes.label: thm:pushpull

nodes.statement: Apply the fixation-limit lemma to the normalized reproductive values, which are invariant and equal to $1$ and $0$ on the two constant configurations; the denominators are positive because every degree is at least $1$.
nodes.section: 60 Push versus pull on arbitrary graphs

nodes.name: Star potential
nodes.statement: For a configuration with $i$ mutant leaves, $\Phi=q^i$ if the centre is a resident and $\Phi=\kappa q^i$ if it is a mutant.
nodes.label: def:star-potential

nodes.name: The star potential is invariant
nodes.statement: For every $r>0$, $\Phi$ is invariant in expectation under one Birth--death step on the star.
nodes.label: thm:star-invariance

nodes.statement: Only the ordered pairs $(c,\ell)$ and $(\ell,c)$ for a leaf $\ell$ carry weight, namely $\mathrm{fit}(c)/(nF)$ and $\mathrm{fit}(\ell)/F$. Along each edge the two contributions cancel: if $\ell$ is a mutant and $c$ a resident they give $\frac{q^{i-1}}F\big(\frac{1-q}n+rq(\kappa-1)\big)=0$, and if $c$ is a mutant and $\ell$ a resident they give $\frac{q^i}F\big(1-\kappa+\frac{r\kappa(q-1)}n\big)=0$; equal types change nothing.

nodes.name: Fixation on the star
nodes.statement: For $r\ne1$, the fixation probability from $s$ is $(1-\Phi(s))/(1-\kappa q^n)$. A single mutant fixes with probability $(1-q)/(1-\kappa q^n)$ from a leaf, $(1-\kappa)/(1-\kappa q^n)$ from the centre, and $(n(1-q)+(1-\kappa))/((n+1)(1-\kappa q^n))$ from a uniformly random vertex.
nodes.label: thm:star

nodes.statement: For $r>1$ we have $q\le1$ and $\kappa<1$, so $\kappa q^n\le\Phi\le1$; for $r<1$ all inequalities reverse. Hence the normalized potential is $1$ at fixation, $0$ at extinction and in $[0,1]$ otherwise, and the fixation-limit lemma applies.

nodes.name: The formula of Broom and Rycht\'a\v{r}
nodes.statement: For every $r>0$, a single mutant at a uniformly random vertex fixes with probability \[ \frac{n\cdot\frac{nr}{nr+1}+\frac r{r+n}}{(n+1)\big(1+\frac n{n+r}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}q^j\big)}. \]
nodes.label: thm:star-sum

nodes.statement: For $r\ne1$ and $n\ge1$, sum the geometric series: $1+\frac n{n+r}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}q^j= r^2(1-\kappa q^n)/(r^2-1)$. For $r=1$ both sides are $1/(n+1)$, by push--pull fixation; for $n=0$ both are $1$.

nodes.name: The star is an amplifier
nodes.statement: For every $n\ge2$, the fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex is larger than Moran's $(1-1/r)/(1-r^{-(n+1)})$ for $r>1$ and smaller for $0<r<1$.
nodes.label: thm:star-amplifier

nodes.statement: Put $s=1/r$ and $t=(1+ns)/(n+s)$, so that $q=st$ and $\kappa=s/t$. The difference has the sign of $(1-s)\big(E(1-s^{n+1})-s^{n+1}(1-t^{n-1})\big)$ with $E=s^2(n-1)^2/((n+s)(1+ns))$. By Bernoulli, $1-t^{n-1}\le(n-1)(1-t)=(n-1)^2(1-s)/(n+s)$, which reduces the claim to $s^{n-1}(1-s)(1+ns)<1-s^{n+1}$. Its slack is $\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}(1-s)(s^k-s^n)$, a nonempty sum of positive terms on both sides of $s=1$.

nodes.name: Large stars amplify $r$ to $r^2$
nodes.statement: For $r>1$, the fixation probability from a uniformly random vertex of the star with $n$ leaves tends to $1-1/r^2$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.label: thm:star-limit

nodes.statement: $n(1-q)/(n+1)=\frac n{n+1}\cdot\frac n{n+1/r}\cdot(1-r^{-2})\to1-r^{-2}$, $(1-\kappa)/(n+1)\to0$, and $0\le\kappa q^n\le r^{-n}\to0$ because $q\le1/r$ for $n\ge1$.

nodes.name: Colorings and color counts
nodes.statement: A \emph{coloring} is a map $x \colon [n] \to [k]$. The number of nodes of color $j$ is $c_j = |\{v : x(v) = j\}|$, and $\sum_j c_j = n$. The vector $c = (c_1,\dots,c_k)$ is the paper's $k$-color distribution ($k$-cd).
nodes.label: def:config

nodes.name: 3-input rules and the 3-majority rule
nodes.statement: A \emph{3-input rule} is a map $f \colon [k]^3 \to [k]$ with $f(a,b,c) \in \{a,b,c\}$. The \emph{3-majority rule} is $\mathrm{maj}_3(a,b,c) = b$ if $b = c$ and $a$ otherwise; it returns the majority color, and the first color if all three differ.
nodes.label: def:rule

nodes.name: One round and the process
nodes.statement: A round is a map $r \colon [n] \to [n]^3$ (the three samples of every node), drawn uniformly. The next coloring under rule $f$ is $v \mapsto f(x(r_v^1), x(r_v^2), x(r_v^3))$. The process after $T$ rounds folds this step over $T$ independent uniform rounds.
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Consensus
nodes.statement: $x$ is in \emph{consensus on $m$} if every node has color $m$, i.e.\ $c_m = n$. For every 3-input rule, consensus is absorbing.
nodes.label: def:mono

nodes.name: The Markov kernel
nodes.statement: The process with rule $f$ is the finite Markov kernel on colorings whose row at $x$ is the law of one round of $f$ from $x$. Its $T$-step event probabilities are the expectations over $T$ independent uniform rounds.
nodes.label: def:kernel

nodes.name: Adoption probability
nodes.statement: The new count of color $j$ is a sum of $n$ independent indicators, one per node. Under 3-majority, a node adopts $j$ with probability $x_j^2 + x_j(1 - \sum_h x_h^2)$, where $x_h = c_h/n$.
nodes.label: lem:adopt

nodes.statement: The three samples are independent with law $(x_h)_h$. Summing the indicator of $\mathrm{maj}_3(a,b,c) = j$ first over $c$, then $b$, then $a$ gives the polynomial.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1, next expected coloring
nodes.statement: For every coloring and every color $j$, \[ \mu_j(c) = \E[C_{j,t+1} \mid C_t = c] = c_j\Bigl(1 + \frac{1}{n^2}\Bigl(n c_j - \sum_h c_h^2\Bigr)\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:2_1

nodes.statement: Multiply the adoption probability of Lemma~\ref{lem:adopt} by $n$.

nodes.name: Section 3 quantities
nodes.statement: For a $k$-cd $c$ with $\sum_h c_h = n$: $m(c) = \max_h c_h$, $M(c) = \{j : c_j = m(c)\}$, the \emph{bias} $s(c) = m(c) - \max_{h \notin M(c)} c_h$ if $|M(c)| = 1$ and $0$ otherwise, $\alpha(c) = (n - m(c))\,s(c)/n^2$ and $\gamma(c) = (n\,m(c) - \sum_h c_h^2)/n^2 - \alpha(c)$.
nodes.label: def:quantities

nodes.name: Every other color trails by the bias
nodes.statement: If $c_m = m(c)$ then $c_h + s(c) \le m(c)$ for every $h \ne m$, with equality for some $h$ when $k \ge 2$. Moreover $\gamma(c)\,n^2 = \sum_{h \ne m} c_h\,(m(c) - s(c) - c_h)$.
nodes.label: lem:bias_gap

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: For every $k$-cd $c$: (a) $0 \le s(c) \le m(c) - (n - m(c))/(k-1)$; (b) $0 \le \alpha(c) \le \min\{s(c)/n,\ 1/4\}$; (c) $0 \le \gamma(c) \le 1/8$.
nodes.label: lem:3_1

nodes.statement: (a) The $k-1$ other colors each have at most $m(c) - s(c)$ nodes. (b) $(n - m)m \le n^2/4$ and $s \le m$. (c) Use the identity of Lemma~\ref{lem:bias_gap}: every summand is nonnegative, the color attaining the bias contributes $0$, and the rest is at most $d(n - m - d) \le n^2/8$ with $d = m(c) - s(c)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: Let $m \in M(c)$ and let $\ell \ne m$ have the most nodes among the other colors. Then (a) $\mu_m(c) = c_m(1 + \gamma + \alpha)$; (b) $\mu_j(c) = c_j(1 + \gamma + \alpha - (m(c) - c_j)/n)$ for every $j$; (c) $\mu_\ell(c) = c_\ell(1 + \gamma + \alpha - s(c)/n)$.
nodes.label: lem:3_2

nodes.name: Concentration for sums of independent coordinates
nodes.statement: For $X = \sum_i Y_i(\omega_i)$ with independent uniform coordinates: Bernstein's inequality $\Pr(X \ge \E X + \lambda) \le \exp(-\lambda^2/(2\sigma^2(1 + b\lambda/(3\sigma^2))))$ when $Y_i - \E Y_i \le b$ and $\sum_i \mathrm{Var}\,Y_i \le \sigma^2$; Hoeffding's inequality for $\{0,1\}$ coordinates; the multiplicative Chernoff lower tail $\Pr(X \le (1-\delta)\mu) \le \exp(-\delta^2\mu/2)$; Markov's inequality $\Pr(X \ge 1) \le \E X$ for nonnegative coordinates; and the closed-form Chernoff upper tail $\Pr(X \ge k) \le \exp(k - \mu - k\log(k/\mu))$ for $\E X \le \mu \le k$. All are proved once in the shared \texttt{dynamics} library (\texttt{Dynamics/Concentration.lean}, \texttt{Dynamics/Chernoff.lean}, \texttt{Dynamics/Tail.lean}).
nodes.label: lem:tails

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3, increasing rate of the bias
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$ then for every $j \ne m$, \[ \Pr\Bigl(C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1} \le s(c)\Bigl(1 + \gamma(c) + \frac{c_m\alpha(c)}{2s(c)}\Bigr) \Bigm| C_t = c\Bigr) \le \exp\Bigl(-\frac{c_m\alpha(c)^2}{25}\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:3_3

nodes.statement: By Lemmas~\ref{lem:3_1} and~\ref{lem:3_2}, $\E[C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1}] \ge s(1+\gamma) + c_m\alpha$. The difference is a sum of per-node variables in $\{-1,0,1\}$ with variance at most $3c_m$; apply Bernstein's inequality with $b = 2$ and $\lambda = c_m\alpha/2$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$ then $\Pr(C_{m,t+1} \le c_m(1 + \gamma + \alpha/2) \mid C_t = c) \le \exp(-c_m\alpha^2/11)$.
nodes.label: lem:3_4

nodes.statement: The multiplicative Chernoff lower tail with $\delta = \alpha/(2(1 + \gamma + \alpha))$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.5, large plurality and large bias
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$, $0 < \lambda \le 2/3$, $\lambda n \le c_m \le (2/3)n$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{(1/\lambda)\,n\log n}$, then for every $j \ne m$ \[ \Pr\bigl(C_{m,t+1} - C_{j,t+1} \le s(c)(1 + \lambda/6)\bigr) \le 1/n^2 \quad\text{and}\quad \Pr\bigl(C_{m,t+1} \le c_m\bigr) \le 1/n^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:3_5

nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses $c_m\alpha/(2s) \ge \lambda/6$ and $c_m\alpha^2/25 \ge 2\log n$; conclude with Lemmas~\ref{lem:3_3} and~\ref{lem:3_4}.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: For every $m \in M(c)$, writing $\bar C_{m,t+1} = n - C_{m,t+1}$, \[ (n - c_m)\Bigl(1 - \frac{c_m^2}{n^2}\Bigr) \le \E[\bar C_{m,t+1} \mid C_t = c] \le (n - c_m)\Bigl(1 - \frac{s(c)\,c_m}{n^2}\Bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:3_6

nodes.name: Lemma 3.7, very large plurality
nodes.statement: Let $\log n \ge 40$, $M(c) = \{m\}$. (i) If $s(c) \ge n/3$ and $n - c_m \ge n^{1/4}\log n$ then $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} \ge \frac{17}{18}(n - c_m)) \le 1/n^2$. (ii) If $n - c_m < n^{1/4}\log n$ then $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} > 0) \le n^{-1/5}$ and $\Pr(\bar C_{m,t+1} \ge n^{1/4}\log n) \le 1/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:3_7

nodes.statement: The paper omits this proof. (i) By Lemma~\ref{lem:3_6} and $s\,c_m \ge n^2/9$, $\E\bar C_{m,t+1} \le \frac89(n - c_m)$; apply the closed-form Chernoff upper tail at ratio $17/16$. (ii) Here $s(c) \ge n - 2(n - c_m)$, so $\E\bar C_{m,t+1} \le 3(n-c_m)^2/n \le 3\log^2 n\, e^{-(\log n)/2}$; apply Markov's inequality for the first bound and the Chernoff upper tail for the second.

nodes.name: Lemma A.4, nested phases
nodes.statement: Let $A_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq A_T$ be sets of states of a finite Markov chain such that from every state of $A_i$ the chain stays in $A_i$ with probability $\ge 1-\varepsilon$ and, for $i < T$, moves into $A_{i+1}$ with probability $\ge 1 - \nu$. Then from any state of $A_1$, after $\ell T$ steps the chain is in $A_T$ with probability at least $1 - T(\ell\varepsilon + \nu^\ell)$.
nodes.label: lem:A_4

nodes.statement: The paper omits this proof. Phase by phase: within $\ell$ steps the chain leaves $A_i$ with probability at most $\ell\varepsilon$, and fails to jump into $A_{i+1}$ in each of the $\ell$ steps with probability at most $\nu^\ell$. The hypothesis $\varepsilon \le \nu$ of the paper is not needed.

nodes.name: The phases
nodes.statement: Fix $m$, $\lambda$, $\Lambda$ and let $q = 1 + 1/(6\lambda)$, $B = n^{1/4}\log n$. \emph{Growth phase $i$}: $c_m > \frac23 n$, or $M(c) = \{m\}$, $c_m \ge n/\lambda$ and $s(c) \ge \Lambda q^i$. \emph{Saturation phase $j$}: $n - c_m < \max\{\frac n3 (\frac{17}{18})^j,\ B\}$. \emph{Consensus}: $c_m = n$.
nodes.label: def:phases

nodes.statement: The paper's saturation phases also require $s(c) \ge n/3$, which Lemma~\ref{lem:3_7} does not show to be preserved. Here the saturation phases only bound $n - c_m < n/3$, which already implies $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge n/3$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:dissent}).

nodes.name: A clear majority
nodes.statement: If $n - c_m < n/3$ then $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge n/3$. If $m$ leads every other color by at least $g > 0$ and $c_m \ge g$, then $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge g$. A color without nodes stays without nodes.
nodes.label: lem:dissent

nodes.name: One round of each phase
nodes.statement: Let $\log n \ge 40$, $k \ge 2$, $\lambda \ge 3$ and $\Lambda \ge 22\sqrt{\lambda n \log n}$. From growth phase $i$ the chain enters growth phase $i+1$ with probability $\ge 1 - 1/n$. From saturation phase $j$ it enters saturation phase $j+1$ with probability $\ge 1 - 1/n^2$. From fewer than $B$ dissenting nodes it reaches consensus with probability $\ge 1 - n^{-1/5}$, and consensus is kept with probability $1$. The phase sets are nested, and growth phase $i$ lies in saturation phase $0$ once $\Lambda q^i > n$.
nodes.label: lem:phase_steps

nodes.statement: \emph{Growth, case $c_m > \frac23 n$}: saturation phase $0$ moves into saturation phase $1$, which lies in $\{c_m > \frac23 n\}$. \emph{Growth, otherwise}: apply Lemma~\ref{lem:3_5} with $1/\lambda$ to each other color $j$ that currently has a node, and to the growth of $c_m$. There are fewer than $n - c_m$ such colors, so a union bound gives failure probability at most $n/n^2$. Colors without nodes stay empty, and the color attaining the bias has a node (otherwise $c_m = n$), so after a successful round $m$ leads every other color by $s(c)\,q$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:dissent} applies. \emph{Saturation}: Lemma~\ref{lem:3_7}(i) above $B$ dissenters and Lemma~\ref{lem:3_7}(ii) below.

nodes.name: Number of phases
nodes.statement: With $T_1 = \lceil \log n/\log q\rceil$ growth phases, $T_2 = \lceil \log n/\log(18/17)\rceil + 1$ saturation phases and one consensus phase, $T = T_1 + T_2 + 1 \le 13\lambda\log n$ for $\lambda \ge 3$ and $\log n \ge 40$.
nodes.label: lem:phases

nodes.statement: $\log(1+x) \ge x/(1+x)$ gives $\log q \ge 1/(6\lambda+1)$ and $\log(18/17) \ge 1/18$.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.8, the general upper bound
nodes.statement: Let $\log n \ge 40$, $k \ge 2$ and $\lambda \ge 3$. If $M(c) = \{m\}$, $c_m \ge n/\lambda$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{\lambda n\log n}$, then after $10T \le 130\lambda\log n$ rounds all nodes support $m$ with probability at least $1 - 11T/n \ge 1 - 143\lambda\log n/n$.
nodes.label: thm:3_8

nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:A_4} to the kernel of 3-majority with the $T_1$ growth phases, the $T_2$ saturation phases and consensus, $\varepsilon = 1/n$, $\nu = n^{-1/5}$ and $\ell = 10$, so that $\nu^\ell = n^{-2}$. The initial coloring is in growth phase $0$; growth phase $T_1$ lies in saturation phase $0$ because $\Lambda q^{T_1} \ge 22n$; saturation phase $T_2 - 1$ lies below $B$ dissenters because $\frac n3(\frac{17}{18})^{T_2-1} \le \frac13$.

The paper states the failure probability as $11T/n^2$; the extra factor $n$ comes from the union bound over competing colors in Lemma~\ref{lem:phase_steps}, which the paper omits. The paper's hypothesis $\lambda < \sqrt n$ is not used; it only makes the hypothesis on $s(c)$ satisfiable.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.10
nodes.statement: If $M(c) = \{m\}$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{\min\{2k, (n/\log n)^{1/3}\}\,n\log n}$, then 3-majority reaches consensus on $m$ in $O(\min\{2k, (n/\log n)^{1/3}\}\log n)$ rounds w.h.p. Precisely, for $\log n \ge 40$ and $k \ge 2$: at most $130\lambda\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 143\lambda\log n/n$.
nodes.label: cor:3_10

nodes.statement: Take $\lambda = \min\{2k, (n/\log n)^{1/3}\}$. If $\lambda = 2k$ then $c_m \ge n/k$ by pigeonhole; otherwise $\lambda^3 = n/\log n$, so $22\sqrt{\lambda n\log n} = 22n/\lambda$ and $c_m \ge s(c) \ge n/\lambda$. Moreover $\lambda \ge 3$ because $k \ge 2$ and $n = e^{\log n} \ge 27\log n$.

nodes.name: Corollaries 3.11 and 3.12
nodes.statement: If $c_m \ge n/\log^\ell n$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{n\log^{\ell+1}n}$, consensus takes $O(\log^{\ell+1} n)$ rounds w.h.p. If $c_m \ge n/\beta$ and $s(c) \ge 22\sqrt{\beta n\log n}$ for a constant $\beta \ge 3$, it takes $O(\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.label: cor:3_11

nodes.statement: Take $\lambda = \log^\ell n$ (with $\ell \ge 1$, so that $\lambda \ge 3$) and $\lambda = \beta$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:3_8}.

nodes.name: Binary case
nodes.statement: With $k = 2$ the set of nodes of color $1$ evolves exactly as the binary 3-majority process of the \texttt{three\_majority} package. Hence, if $c_1 \ge \frac35 n$ and $\log n \ge 30$, all nodes support color $1$ after $O(\log n)$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 500/n$.
nodes.label: thm:binary

nodes.name: Two opinions from a vanishing bias
nodes.statement: In the binary 3-majority process, if the initial majority leads by at least $22\sqrt{3n\log n}$ nodes (a fraction $\frac12 + O(\sqrt{\log n/n})$) and $\log n \ge 40$, all nodes adopt it within at most $390\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 429\log n/n$.
nodes.label: cor:binary_vanishing

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:3_8} with $k = 2$ and $\lambda = 3$: the majority color is the unique plurality, holds more than $n/2 \ge n/3$ nodes, and its bias is the gap; the conclusion transfers to the binary process through Theorem~\ref{thm:binary}.

nodes.name: Jump near balance
nodes.statement: If $n \ge 5$ and $|s| \le 4\sqrt n/25$, then $|s'| \ge \sqrt n/5$ with probability at least $9/64$.
nodes.label: lem:jump_near_balance

nodes.statement: The centered sum $S = \sum_v (Y_v - p)$ has variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p) \ge n/5$ and fourth moment at most $\sigma^2 + 3\sigma^4$, so by Paley--Zygmund $4S^2 \ge \sigma^2$ with probability at least $9/64$. Then $|s'| = |2S + \mathbb{E}s'| \ge \sqrt{n/5} - \frac32|s| \ge \sqrt n/5$.

nodes.name: Growth away from balance
nodes.statement: If $0 \le s \le n/2$ and $\lambda \ge 0$, then $s' > \frac{11}{8}s - 2\lambda$ with probability at least $1 - e^{-2\lambda^2/n}$.
nodes.label: lem:growth_far

nodes.statement: $\mathbb{E}s' \ge \frac{11}{8}s$ for $0 \le s \le n/2$, and Hoeffding's inequality bounds the lower tail of $\sum_v Y_v$.

nodes.name: Symmetry breaking
nodes.statement: There is $C > 0$ such that, for $\log n \ge 40$, from any configuration the gap reaches $22\sqrt{3n\log n}$ in absolute value within any $t \ge C\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - 1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:symmetry_breaking

nodes.statement: Apply the hitting-time bound of Doerr et al.\ (their Claim~2.9, \texttt{Dynamics.Kernel.drift\_hitting\_log}) to $X = \lfloor |s|/(\sqrt n/100)\rfloor$ with $q = n$, $c_1 = 5/4$, $c_2 = 1/320000$, $c_3 = 9/64$, $c_4 = 1000$, $c_6 = 1$; by the symmetry between the opinions assume $s \ge 0$. If $X = 0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:jump_near_balance} gives $X' \ge 20 \ge 1$ with probability $9/64$. If $1 \le X < 16$, the same lemma gives $X' \ge 20 \ge \frac54 X$ with probability $9/64 \ge 1 - e^{-X/320000}$. If $16 \le X < 1000\log n$, then $s \le n/2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:growth_far} with $\lambda = X\sqrt n/3200$ gives $s' > \frac{21}{16}X\sqrt n/100$, hence $X' \ge \frac54 X$, except with probability $e^{-X^2/5120000} \le e^{-X/320000}$. Reaching $X \ge 1000\log n$ means $|s| \ge 10\sqrt n\log n \ge 22\sqrt{3n\log n}$.

nodes.name: Hit, then absorb
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an absorbing event of a finite Markov chain. If from every state of $B$ the chain is in $P$ after $T$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$, then from any state it is in $P$ at time $t + T$ with probability at least $\Pr(T_B \le t) - \varepsilon$. If moreover from every state the chain is in $P$ after $T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \varepsilon$, and from $a$ after $T_0$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta$, then from $a$ it is in $P$ after $T_0 + T_1$ steps with probability at least $1 - \delta\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: lem:hit_absorb

nodes.statement: The first claim by induction on $t$, through the recursion of $\Pr(T_B \le t)$ and the monotonicity in time of an absorbing event; the second by the Markov property at time $T_0$.

nodes.name: Two opinions from any configuration
nodes.statement: There is $C > 0$ such that, for $\log n \ge 40$, from any configuration (in particular from a perfectly balanced one) all nodes hold the same opinion after any $T \ge C\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1 - C\log n/n$; and, for $\log n \ge C$, with probability at least $1 - 1/n$.
nodes.label: thm:any_start

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetry_breaking}, then Corollary~\ref{cor:binary_vanishing} applied to the set of nodes of opinion $1$ or to its complement, composed by Lemma~\ref{lem:hit_absorb}; consensus on either opinion is absorbing, so further rounds keep it. For the second bound, two consecutive blocks each fail with probability at most $\varepsilon = C_0\log n/n$, and $\varepsilon^2 \le 1/n$.

nodes.name: Escaping a moving target
nodes.statement: If a round-based process starts in $G_0$ and, for every $t < T$, one round from any state of $G_t$ misses $G_{t+1}$ with probability at most $p$, then after $T$ rounds it lies outside $G_T$ with probability at most $Tp$.
nodes.label: lem:escape

nodes.statement: Induction on $T$, conditioning on the first round.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Let $k\sqrt{n\log n} \le b \le n/k$. If $c_j \le n/k + b$, then $\Pr(C_{j,t+1} \ge n/k + (1 + 3/k)b \mid C_t = c) \le 1/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:4_1

nodes.statement: By Cauchy--Schwarz $\sum_h c_h^2 \ge n^2/k$, so $\mu_j \le c_j(1 + c_j/n - 1/k)$. Writing $c_j = n/k + a$ with $a \le b$, this is at most $n/k + (1+1/k)b + b^2/n \le n/k + (1+2/k)b$. Hoeffding's inequality with deviation $b/k \ge \sqrt{n\log n}$ gives $1/n^2$.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.2, lower bound for 3-majority
nodes.statement: Let $k \ge 3$ and suppose every color starts with at most $n/k + b$ nodes, where $b \ge k\sqrt{n\log n}$. If $b(1 + 3/k)^T \le n/k$, in particular if $T \le \frac k3 \log\frac{n}{kb}$, then the coloring after $T$ rounds is monochromatic with probability at most $kT/n^2$.
nodes.label: thm:4_2

nodes.statement: For each color apply Lemma~\ref{lem:escape} to the thresholds $n/k + b(1+3/k)^t$, with Lemma~\ref{lem:4_1} for each round. A monochromatic coloring has a color with $n > 2n/k$ nodes, above its final threshold; sum over the $k$ colors.

With $b = \max\{(n/k)^{1-\varepsilon}, k\sqrt{n\log n}\}$ this gives $\Omega(k\log(n/(kb)))$ rounds, which is $\Omega(k\log n)$ for $k \le n^{1/4-\delta}$. The paper states $\Omega(k\log n)$ for all $k \le (n/\log n)^{1/4}$, but at that end $n/k = k\sqrt{n\log n}$ and the argument gives nothing. The paper's proof also chooses the thresholds after seeing the trajectory; the union bound needs the fixed schedule used here.

nodes.name: Rules, $\Delta$, $\delta$ and solvers
nodes.statement: A rule is \emph{conservative} if it returns one of its inputs. It has the \emph{clear-majority} property if it returns the majority color whenever two inputs agree. For colors $r \ne b$, $\Delta_r$ counts the orderings of $(r,r,b)$ on which the rule returns $r$. For distinct $r,g,b$, $\delta_c$ counts the orderings of $(r,g,b)$ on which it returns $c$; the rule is \emph{uniform} if $\delta_r = 2$ for all distinct triples. It is an \emph{$(s,\varepsilon)$-solver} if from every coloring whose unique plurality color $m$ has bias at least $s$, consensus on $m$ is eventually reached with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: def:good_rules

nodes.name: Consensus needs survival
nodes.statement: Under a conservative rule a color without nodes never returns. Hence for all $T, T_0$, the probability of consensus on $m$ at time $T$ is at most the probability that $m$ has a node at time $T_0$.
nodes.label: lem:alive

nodes.name: Theorem 4.8(a), clear majority
nodes.statement: Let $8 \mid n$. With only colors $r, b$ present and $x$ the fraction of $r$, a node adopts $r$ with probability $p(x)$, where $p(x) - x = x(1-x)\bigl(x(\Delta_r - 2) + (1-x)(2 - \Delta_b)\bigr)$. If $\Delta_r \le 2 \le \Delta_b$, the number of $r$ nodes is a supermartingale, so from $5n/8$ nodes of $r$ (bias $n/4$) consensus on $r$ has probability at most $5/8$ at every time: the rule is not an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver. Consequently, for an $(n/4, 1/4)$-solver and every pair $r \ne b$, either $\Delta_r = \Delta_b = 3$ or $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$.
nodes.label: thm:4_8_a

nodes.statement: $\E[X_T] \le X_0$ by induction on $T$, and $\Pr(X_T = n) \le \E[X_T]/n$.

The paper claims that an $(n/4,1/4)$-solver has the clear-majority property, i.e.\ that $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$ is also impossible. Its proof uses the supermartingale property, but checks it only when red is the majority; for $\Delta_r, \Delta_b \le 1$ it fails when red is the minority, because the process is pulled to the interior point $x^* = (2 - \Delta_b)/(4 - \Delta_r - \Delta_b)$. That case is not formalized.

nodes.name: Adopting $r$ among three colors
nodes.statement: Let the rule be conservative with the clear-majority property, let only $r, g, b$ be present and $\delta_r \le 1$. Then $p(r) \le 3x^2 - 2x^3 + \delta_r x_r x_g x_b \le x(3x - 2x^2 + (1-x)^2/4)$, which is at most $0.97x$ for $x \le 2/5$; and from $x \le 2/5$ one round ends above $2n/5$ with probability at most $e^{-9n/31250}$.
nodes.label: lem:adopt3

nodes.name: $r$ dies out
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:adopt3}, starting with at most $2n/5$ nodes of $r$, the probability that $r$ still has a node after $T$ rounds is at most $0.97^T c_r + T e^{-9n/31250}$.
nodes.label: lem:extinct

nodes.statement: Consider the chain frozen once $r$ exceeds $2n/5$. On it, $\Phi = C_r\,\mathbb 1[C_r \le 2n/5]$ contracts by $0.97$ in every state, it is frozen within $T$ rounds with probability at most $Te^{-9n/31250}$, and it agrees with the real chain until it is frozen.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.8(b), uniform property
nodes.statement: Let $60 \mid n$ and $\log n \ge 20$. A rule with the clear-majority property that is an $(n/20, 1/4)$-solver has the uniform property.
nodes.label: thm:4_8_b

nodes.statement: If a triple is not uniform, some color $r$ of it has $\delta_r \le 1$, since the three counts sum to $6$. Start from $23n/60$ nodes of $r$, $n/3$ of $g$ and $17n/60$ of $b$: $r$ is the unique plurality color with bias $n/20$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:extinct} and~\ref{lem:alive}, with $T_0 = \lceil\log(8n)/\log(100/97)\rceil$, consensus on $r$ has probability at most $1/8 + 1/8$ at every time.

The paper's proof (Lemma 4.10) is a sketch that treats $\delta_r = 1$ with $(\delta_g,\delta_b) \in \{(3,2),(4,1)\}$ and asserts that $r$ ``will not converge'' by iterating a one-round estimate. The proof here covers every non-uniform triple and makes the iteration rigorous.

nodes.name: $h$-plurality
nodes.statement: Every node samples $h$ nodes and a uniformly random ordering $\sigma$ of the $h$ sample positions, and adopts the color of the position of smallest $\sigma$-rank among those whose color is most frequent. All tied colors appear equally often, so each is chosen with the same probability.
nodes.label: def:hplur

nodes.name: Adoption under $h$-plurality
nodes.statement: A node adopts $j$ with probability at most $x_j + \frac{h^2}{2}x_j^2$.
nodes.label: lem:hadopt

nodes.statement: If $j$ wins and is seen exactly once, all $h$ sampled colors are distinct and $j$ is at the position ranked first, which has probability $x_j$. Otherwise $j$ is seen at least twice, and $\Pr(N_j \ge 2) \le \E[N_j(N_j-1)]/2 = \binom h2 x_j^2$.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.11
nodes.statement: If $c_j \le a \le 2n/k$, then $\Pr(C_{j,t+1} \ge a(1 + 2h^2/k)) \le \exp(-2(ah^2/k)^2/n)$, which is at most $e^{-2nh^4/k^4}$ when $a \ge n/k$.
nodes.label: lem:4_11

nodes.statement: The paper states the factor $1 + h^2/k$ but its proof gives $1 + 2h^2/k$, which is also what Theorem~\ref{thm:4_12} uses. Allowing $c_j \le a$ instead of $c_j = a$ covers colors below $n/k$, which the paper's proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:4_12} needs but the lemma excludes.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.12, lower bound for $h$-plurality
nodes.statement: Let $k \ge 3$. If every color starts with at most $\frac32\cdot\frac nk$ nodes and $T \le \frac{k}{2h^2}\log\frac43$, then after $T$ rounds of $h$-plurality the coloring is monochromatic with probability at most $kT e^{-2nh^4/k^4}$.
nodes.label: thm:4_12

nodes.statement: As for Theorem~\ref{thm:4_2}, with thresholds $\frac32\cdot\frac nk(1 + 2h^2/k)^t \le 2n/k$.

nodes.name: Round randomness
nodes.statement: A \emph{round configuration} is a function $\omega \colon V \to V$ with $\omega(v) \ne v$ for all $v$. Let $R_n$ denote the (finite) set of round configurations; it carries the uniform probability measure, i.e.\ every node picks a uniformly random \emph{target} among the other $n-1$ nodes, independently of all other nodes.
nodes.label: def:round

nodes.name: Push step
nodes.statement: For an \emph{informed set} $I \subseteq V$ and a round configuration $\omega \in R_n$, the next informed set is \[ \mathrm{step}(I,\omega) \;=\; I \,\cup\, \omega(I) \;=\; I \cup \{\omega(v) : v \in I\}. \] (Only informed nodes actually transmit; letting \emph{all} nodes draw a target and ignoring the choices of uninformed nodes is an equivalent and formalization-friendlier convention.)
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Process
nodes.statement: Fix a horizon $T \in \N$ and a start vertex $v_0 \in V$. The sample space is $\Omega = R_n^{\,T}$ (uniform measure, i.e.\ i.i.d.\ uniform rounds). For $\omega = (\omega_0,\dots,\omega_{T-1}) \in \Omega$ define $I_0(\omega) = \{v_0\}$ and $I_{t+1}(\omega) = \mathrm{step}(I_t(\omega), \omega_t)$ for $0 \le t < T$. We write $m_t = |I_t|$ and $U_t = n - m_t$ for the numbers of informed and uninformed nodes. Since $\Omega$ is finite, all probabilities are finite ratios and all expectations are finite sums; ``conditioning on $I_t$'' means partitioning $\Omega$ according to the first $t$ coordinates. In the formalization, a trajectory is simply a \texttt{List} of round configurations and $\mathrm{run}\ I\ l$ folds \texttt{step} over the list $l$.
nodes.label: def:process

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: $I_t(\omega) \subseteq I_{t+1}(\omega)$ for all $t$ and all $\omega$; hence $m_t$ is non-decreasing and $U_t$ is non-increasing in $t$, pointwise on $\Omega$.
nodes.label: lem:mono

nodes.name: At most doubling
nodes.statement: $|I_{t+1}(\omega) \smallsetminus I_t(\omega)| \le |I_t(\omega)|$; equivalently $(\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)).\mathrm{card} \le 2\,I.\mathrm{card}$.
nodes.label: lem:atmost

nodes.name: Push protocol informs $K_n$ in $O(\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 2$, let $v_0 \in V$, and set \[ T_1 \;=\; \ceil{117 \log n} + 23, \qquad T_2 \;=\; \ceil{6 \log n}, \qquad T \;=\; T_1 + T_2 . \] Then $\Pr\bigl[\, I_T = V \,\bigr] \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{2}{n}$. In particular all nodes are informed after $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.statement: The constants are deliberately crude: the proof is organized to minimize the analytic toolkit, not the round count. The sharp answer is $\log_2 n + \log n + o(\log n)$ (Frieze--Grimmett \cite{FG85}, Pittel \cite{Pittel87}). Replacing $2/n$ by $n^{-\alpha}$ for any fixed $\alpha \ge 1$ only changes the constants in $T_1, T_2$.

nodes.name: Average
nodes.statement: For a finite type $\alpha$ and $f \colon \alpha \to \R$, $\mathrm{avg}(f) := \bigl(\sum_{a} f(a)\bigr) / |\alpha|$ is the expectation of $f$ under the uniform distribution on $\alpha$.
nodes.label: def:avg

nodes.name: Trajectory expectation
nodes.statement: For a finite type $\alpha$, $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ F$ is the expectation of a functional $F$ of a trajectory of $T$ i.i.d.\ uniform draws from $\alpha$, defined \emph{by recursion on $T$}: the head draw is averaged out first, i.e.\ $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ 0\ F = F(\,[]\,)$ and $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ (T{+}1)\ F = \mathrm{avg}\bigl(a \mapsto \mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ (l \mapsto F(a :: l))\bigr)$. This makes ``conditioning on the first round'' a definitional unfolding rather than a measure-theoretic construction.
nodes.label: def:expList

nodes.name: Basic properties
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{avg}$ and $\mathrm{expList}$ are monotone, additive, and homogeneous, and constants pass through unchanged. These pointwise inequalities pushed through $\mathrm{avg\_le\_avg}$ / $\mathrm{expList\_le\_expList}$ are the only form in which Markov's inequality and union bounds are used below (Lemmas~\ref{lem:markov} and~\ref{lem:revmarkov}); they are not separately formalized lemmas.
nodes.label: lem:avg-basic

nodes.name: Faithfulness of the model
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{expList}\ \alpha\ T\ F$ equals the uniform average of $F$ over \emph{all} length-$T$ sequences of draws, i.e.\ over the product probability space $\mathrm{Fin}\ T \to \alpha$ of $T$ i.i.d.\ uniform rounds. This confirms that the recursive definition of Definition~\ref{def:expList} is the textbook object.
nodes.label: thm:faithful

nodes.name: Bernoulli
nodes.statement: For all real $y \ge -1$ (we only use $y\in[-1,1]$) and $m \in \N$: $(1+y)^m \ge 1 + my$. Equivalently, with $y = -x$: $1 - mx \le (1-x)^m$.
nodes.label: lem:bernoulli

nodes.name: Second-order lower bound, ``Bonferroni''
nodes.statement: For $0 \le x \le 1$ and $m \in \N$: \[ 1-(1-x)^m \;\ge\; mx - \binom{m}{2}x^2 \;\ge\; mx\Bigl(1-\frac{mx}{2}\Bigr), \] and consequently $mx/2 \le 1-(1-x)^m$ whenever $mx \le 1$.
nodes.label: lem:bonferroni

nodes.name: Upper bound without $e$
nodes.statement: For $0 \le x \le 1$ and $m \in \N$: $(1-x)^m \le \dfrac{1}{1+mx}$.
nodes.label: lem:upper

nodes.name: Logarithm bounds
nodes.statement: For $x > 0$: $1 - \tfrac1x \le \log x$. (The formalization only needs this left inequality, applied at $x = 9/8,\ 16/15,\ 3/2$, together with Mathlib's numeric bound $\log 2 < 0.6931471808$.)
nodes.label: lem:logbounds

nodes.name: Markov's inequality, finite uniform version
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set with the uniform measure, $f \colon \Omega \to \R$ with $f \ge 0$, and $a > 0$. Then $\Pr[f \ge a] \le \E[f]/a$. In particular, if $f$ takes values in $\N$, then $\Pr[f \ne 0] \le \E[f]$.
nodes.label: lem:markov

nodes.name: Reverse Markov for bounded variables
nodes.statement: Let $f \colon \Omega \to \R$ with $0 \le f \le b$ pointwise, $b > 0$, and let $0 < a < b$. Then $\Pr[f \ge a] \ge \dfrac{\E[f] - a}{b}$. (As with Lemma~\ref{lem:markov}, the formalization does not isolate this as a named lemma: each use site supplies its own pointwise bound and pushes it through $\mathrm{avg\_le\_avg}$, e.g.\ in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround}.)
nodes.label: lem:revmarkov

nodes.name: Contact probability
nodes.statement: For any fixed $u \notin I$, \[ \Pr_\omega\bigl[u \in \mathrm{step}(I,\omega)\bigr] \;=\; 1 - \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{n-1}\Bigr)^{m}. \] The Lean proof is the only place where a probability is \emph{computed} rather than estimated: it counts round configurations avoiding $u$ on $I$ via an explicit equivalence to a product of subtypes and \texttt{Fintype.card\_pi}.
nodes.label: lem:contact

nodes.name: Expected growth
nodes.statement: Let $N(\omega) = |\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)| - m$ be the number of newly informed nodes. The formalization gives the \emph{exact} formula \[ \E_\omega[|\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)|] \;=\; m + (n-m)\bigl(1-(1-x)^m\bigr), \] from which, if $1 \le m \le n/2$: $\E_\omega[N] \ge m/4$ (using Lemma~\ref{lem:bonferroni} and $n - m \ge n/2$, $mx \le 1$).
nodes.label: lem:expgrowth

nodes.name: A good round has constant probability
nodes.statement: If $1 \le m \le n/2$, then $\Pr_\omega\bigl[\,|\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)| \ge \tfrac{9}{8}\,m\,\bigr] \ge \tfrac18$.
nodes.label: lem:goodround

nodes.name: Contraction above half
nodes.statement: If $m \ge n/2$, then for every fixed $u \notin I$, $\Pr_\omega[u \notin \mathrm{step}(I,\omega)] = (1-x)^m \le \tfrac23$, and consequently, with $U' := n - |\mathrm{step}(I,\omega)|$, $\E_\omega[U'] \le \tfrac23(n-m)$.
nodes.label: lem:contract

nodes.name: Good rounds
nodes.statement: A round is \emph{good} if it multiplies the informed set by $\ge 9/8$, or if the informed set already exceeds $n/2$: \[ X_t \;=\; \mathbf{1}\Bigl[\, m_{t+1} \ge \tfrac98\, m_t \;\;\text{or}\;\; m_t > \tfrac n2 \,\Bigr] \in \{0,1\}. \] $\mathrm{goodCount}$ counts the good rounds along a trajectory. By Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround} (applied when $m_t \le n/2$; trivial otherwise), $\Pr[X_t = 1 \mid \omega_0,\dots,\omega_{t-1}] \ge \tfrac18$ for every prefix, since $\omega_t$ is independent of the prefix and $\mathrm{expList}$ conditions on it definitionally.
nodes.label: def:good

nodes.name: Exponential moment for adaptive trials
nodes.statement: For every $T$ and every nonempty $I$, \[ \E\Bigl[\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^{\mathrm{goodCount}(I,\,\cdot\,)}\Bigr] \;\le\; \Bigl(\frac{15}{16}\Bigr)^{T} \] over $T$ rounds started at $I$. (This specializes the textbook ``$\E[s^G] \le (1-p(1-s))^T$ for adaptive $\{0,1\}$-trials with per-step success probability $\ge p$'' at $p = 1/8$, $s = 1/2$; the formalization proves the specialized statement directly by induction on $T$ rather than the general one, since only this instance is needed. The ensuing tail bound $\Pr[G < L] \le 2^{L}(15/16)^{T}$ — via $s^{L}\Pr[G<L] \le \E[s^G]$ — is likewise not isolated as a separate lemma; it is proved inline inside Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1} (\texttt{phase1}).
nodes.label: lem:adaptive

nodes.name: Enough good rounds force half-saturation
nodes.statement: Let $L \in \N$ satisfy $(9/8)^L > n/2$. If the informed set never exceeds $n/2$ up to time $T_1$, then along that trajectory $m_{T_1} \ge (9/8)^{\mathrm{goodCount}} \cdot m_0$: every good round multiplies $m_t$ by $\ge 9/8$ and every round is non-decreasing (Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}), so $\mathrm{goodCount} \ge L$ would force $m_{T_1} > n/2$, a contradiction — hence $\mathrm{goodCount} < L \Rightarrow m_{T_1} \le n/2$ is impossible to rule out only via the deterministic growth bound stated here.
nodes.label: lem:force

nodes.name: Phase 1
nodes.statement: If $(9/8)^L \ge n$, then after $T_1$ rounds the informed set is still $\le n/2$ with probability at most $2^{L}\,(15/16)^{T_1}$.
nodes.label: lem:phase1

nodes.name: Admissible constants
nodes.statement: With $L = \ceil{9 \log n} + 1$ we have $(9/8)^L \ge n$ (\texttt{numeric\_A}), and with $T_1 = \ceil{117 \log n} + 23$ we have $2^{L}(15/16)^{T_1} \le 1/n$ (\texttt{numeric\_B}), using $\log\tfrac98 \ge \tfrac19$, $\log\tfrac{16}{15} \ge \tfrac1{16}$ and $\log 2 < 0.6932$. Combined with Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1}: $\Pr[m_{T_1} \le n/2] \le 1/n$. The clean statement to formalize is that \emph{any} $L, T_1$ satisfying these two numeric inequalities work; the values above merely exhibit admissible ones.
nodes.label: lem:constants

nodes.name: Phase 2
nodes.statement: Let $A = \{m_{T_1} > n/2\}$ (an event determined by the first $T_1$ coordinates). Then for every $s \ge 0$, $\E\bigl[\, U_{T_1 + s}\, \mathbf{1}_A \,\bigr] \le (2/3)^{s}\, n$, by induction on $s$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:contract} at each step (monotonicity keeps $m_{T_1+s} > n/2$ on $A$).
nodes.label: lem:phase2

nodes.statement: With $T_2 = \ceil{6 \log n}$: $\Pr[\, U_T \ge 1 \text{ and } A \,] \le n\,(2/3)^{T_2} \le 1/n$. ($U_T$ is $\N$-valued, so Markov applied to $U_T \mathbf{1}_A$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:phase2} give the first inequality; $(2/3)^{T_2} n \le 1/n$ — \texttt{numeric\_C} — follows from $\log\tfrac32 \ge \tfrac13$ and $T_2 \ge 6\log n$.)
nodes.label: lem:phase2cor

nodes.name: Gluing the two phases
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{prNotAllInformed}(n,v_0,T)$ be the probability that some node is still uninformed after $T$ rounds started at $v_0$. For all $L, T_1, T_2$ with $(9/8)^L \le n$: \[ \mathrm{prNotAllInformed}(n,v_0,T_1+T_2) \;\le\; 2^{L}\Bigl(\frac{15}{16}\Bigr)^{T_1} + \Bigl(\frac23\Bigr)^{T_2} n. \] Failure requires either phase 1 to fail (informed set still $\le n/2$ after $T_1$ rounds, Lemma~\ref{lem:phase1}) or phase 2 to leave an uninformed node on the complementary event, controlled by Lemma~\ref{lem:phase2} via Markov.
nodes.label: lem:gluing

nodes.name: PULL and PUSH--PULL rounds
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{pullStep}(I,\omega) = I \cup \{v : \omega(v) \in I\}$ and $\mathrm{pushPullStep}(I,\omega) = \mathrm{step}(I,\omega) \cup \mathrm{pullStep}(I,\omega)$; trajectories fold these steps over a list of i.i.d.\ uniform rounds, and the failure probabilities are the probabilities that some node is still uninformed after $T$ rounds started from $\{v_0\}$.
nodes.label: def:pull

nodes.name: Pathwise domination
nodes.statement: With the same calls, the PUSH--PULL informed set contains the PUSH and the PULL informed sets after every number of rounds.
nodes.label: lem:pull-domination

nodes.name: Independent calls
nodes.statement: The calls $\omega(v)$, $v \in V$, of a uniform round are independent, each uniform among the other $n-1$ nodes; in particular a caller $v \notin I$ calls into $I$ with probability $|I|/(n-1)$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-indep

nodes.name: One PULL or PUSH--PULL round, exactly
nodes.statement: Let $m = |I|$ and $u = n - m$. From a single informed node a PULL round informs nobody with probability $(1 - \frac1{n-1})^{n-1}$. After one PULL round, $\E|I'| = m + u\,\frac{m}{n-1}$ and $\E[n - |I'|] = \frac{u(u-1)}{n-1} \le \frac{u^2}{n}$ (quadratic shrinking). After one PUSH--PULL round, $\E[n - |I'|] = \frac{u(u-1)}{n-1}\bigl(1 - \frac1{n-1}\bigr)^{m}$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-oneround

nodes.name: The two-phase argument for any inflationary step
nodes.statement: Let $f(I,a) \supseteq I$ be a spreading step driven by i.i.d.\ uniform rounds $a$. Suppose that from every nonempty $I$ a round is good ($|f(I,a)| \ge \frac98 |I|$, or $|I| > n/2$) with probability at least $1/8$, and that for $|I| \ge n/2$ the expected number of uninformed nodes contracts by $2/3$. Then after $\ceil{160 \log n}$ rounds from $\{v_0\}$, some node is uninformed with probability at most $2/n$. The proof is the PUSH proof of Sections~\ref{sec:adaptive}--\ref{sec:proof-main}, which uses no other property of $\mathrm{step}$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-phases

nodes.name: The two inputs for PULL
nodes.statement: A PULL round is good with probability at least $1/8$, and for $|I| \ge n/2$ it contracts the expected uninformed count by $2/3$.
nodes.label: lem:pull-good

nodes.statement: The contraction follows from $\frac{u(u-1)}{n-1} \le \frac23 u$ for $u \le n/2$. For good rounds, let $X$ be the number of uninformed callers that call into $I$, so $|I'| = |I| + X$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-indep}, $\mu = \E X = \frac{(n-m)m}{n-1} \ge \max(m/2, 1/2)$ for $m \le n/2$ and, the calls being pairwise independent, $\E X^2 \le \mu + \mu^2$. A round that is not good has $X < m/8 \le \mu/4$, so pointwise $X \le \mu/4 + X^2/(2t) + (t/2)\,\mathbf 1[\text{good}]$ with $t = 4(1+\mu)/3$; taking expectations gives $\Pr[\text{good}] \ge \frac{3\mu}{4t} \ge 3/16$ (a Paley--Zygmund bound). Unlike PUSH, the reverse Markov argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:goodround} does not apply, since a PULL round can inform many more than $|I|$ new nodes.

nodes.name: PULL and PUSH--PULL inform $K_n$ in $O(\log n)$ rounds w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 2$ and $v_0 \in V$. After $\ceil{160 \log n}$ rounds of PULL, or of PUSH--PULL, started from $\{v_0\}$, all nodes are informed with probability at least $1 - 2/n$.
nodes.label: thm:pull

nodes.statement: For PULL, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-phases} with the inputs of Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-good}. For PUSH--PULL, the failure event is contained in the PULL failure event by Lemma~\ref{lem:pull-domination}.

nodes.name: Undecided-state dynamics
nodes.statement: Each of $n$ nodes holds opinion $a$, opinion $b$, or is undecided. In a round every node samples a node uniformly at random (with replacement, possibly itself): an undecided node adopts the sampled opinion, and a decided node that samples the other opinion becomes undecided. We write $a$, $b$, $q$ for the numbers of $a$-, $b$- and undecided nodes.
nodes.label: def:usd

nodes.name: Per-node probabilities
nodes.statement: The state of a node after a round depends only on the node it samples, which is uniform; so an $a$-node stays $a$ with probability $1-b/n$ and an undecided node becomes $a$ with probability $a/n$.
nodes.label: lem:node

nodes.statement: The average over all sampling functions of a function of one coordinate is the uniform average.

nodes.name: Expected counts and bias
nodes.statement: After one round, the expected numbers of $a$-, $b$- and undecided nodes are $a(n-b+q)/n$, $b(n-a+q)/n$ and $(q^2+2ab)/n$; hence the expected bias is $(a-b)(1+q/n)$.
nodes.label: thm:expect

nodes.statement: Sum Lemma~\ref{lem:node} over the nodes; $a(n-b+q)-b(n-a+q)=(a-b)(n+q)$.

nodes.name: Almost-sure absorption
nodes.statement: Monochromatic configurations are fixed points, and from every configuration the probability of not being monochromatic after $t$ rounds tends to $0$.
nodes.label: thm:absorbed

nodes.statement: If some node $w$ is decided, the round in which everybody samples $w$, repeated twice, makes the configuration monochromatic; it has positive probability. Conclude with the shared absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Bad rounds
nodes.statement: A round is bad with probability at most $4e^{-2\Lambda^2/n}=4/n^2$.
nodes.label: lem:badround

nodes.statement: Each count after the round is a sum of independent indicators, one per node, depending only on the node it samples; apply Hoeffding's inequality to the four tails.

nodes.name: Good rounds
nodes.statement: After a good round, $s'>s(1+q/n)-2\Lambda$ and $q'>n/3-s^2/(2n)-\Lambda$. If $b+2q\le 2n/3$ and $q\le n/3$, the potential $\Psi=12b+q$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\Psi']\le\frac56\Psi$, hence $\Psi'<\frac56\Psi+13\Lambda$ after a good round.
nodes.label: lem:goodround

nodes.name: Phases
nodes.statement: Let $2000\Lambda\le n$ and $p=4/n^2$. (Growth) From $s\ge 402\Lambda$, after $T+1$ rounds $s\ge\min(400\Lambda(201/200)^T,7n/10)$ except with probability $(T+1)p$. (Bridge) From $s\ge 7n/10$, after $18$ rounds $\Psi\le n/3$ except with probability $18p$. (Final) From $\Psi\le n/3$, not all nodes hold $a$ after $T$ rounds with probability at most $(5/6)^T\Psi+Tp$.
nodes.label: thm:phases

nodes.statement: Growth: the sets $\{s\ge g,\ (q\ge n/100\text{ or }s\ge g+n/20)\}$ are entered with $g=400\Lambda$ after one good round and $g$ grows by $201/200$ per good round (if $s\le 4n/5$ then $q'\ge n/100$); union bound over rounds with moving targets. Bridge: while $s\ge 2n/3$, $\Psi$ shrinks by $9/10$ per good round and $s$ loses at most $2\Lambda$. Final: induction on $T$, splitting on whether the first round stays in $\{\Psi\le n/3\}$; and $\Psi\ge 1$ unless all nodes hold $a$.

nodes.name: Majority phase
nodes.statement: Let $C=10^4$. For every $n$ with $\log n\ge C$ and every configuration (any number of undecided nodes) with $|a-b|\ge C\sqrt{n\log n}$, all nodes hold the initial majority opinion after $\lceil C\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-2/n$. Without undecided nodes and with $a\ge(1+\alpha)b$, the same holds with a constant depending on $\alpha$ (SODA 2015, Theorem~11 for two colours).
nodes.label: thm:majority

nodes.statement: Run $T_1+1$ growth rounds with $T_1=\lceil\log n/\log(201/200)\rceil$, $18$ bridge rounds and the remaining $T_3\ge 12\log n$ final rounds, so that $(5/6)^{T_3}\le n^{-2}$; the failure probability is at most $\lceil C\log n\rceil p+n^{-2}\cdot n/3\le 2/n$. A $b$-majority follows by exchanging the opinions. With $a\ge(1+\alpha)b$ and $q=0$ the bias is at least $\alpha n/(2+\alpha)$, which exceeds $C\sqrt{n\log n}$ once $\log n\ge C(1+3(2+\alpha)/\alpha)$; extra rounds do not hurt since the all-$a$ configuration is absorbing.

nodes.name: Model
nodes.statement: Equations (3)--(4) hold, $1\le\mathrm{md}(c)\le k$, and the two-colour dynamics is the binary dynamics under undecided $\mapsto u$, colour $0\mapsto a$, colour $1\mapsto b$.
nodes.label: thm:pmodel

nodes.statement: Linearity over the nodes, as in the binary case; the binary update is checked on the nine pairs of states.

nodes.name: Good rounds
nodes.statement: Let $\ell=3\log n$ and call a round good if every count is within $\sqrt{3\ell(\mu+2\ell)}$ of its mean $\mu$ (Bernstein); a round is bad with probability at most $(k+4)/n^3$. Let $\theta=1/(1+\alpha)$, $\kappa=1-\theta$, $B=2\,\mathrm{md}(x_0)$, $S$ the nodes of colours other than $m$, $c=c_m$, $\Phi=\mu_m$. If $n\ge 2\cdot10^{12}K^2k^3\log n$ with $K=(1+\alpha)^2/\alpha$, a good round keeps the invariant $c_i+12\sqrt{\ell c}\le\theta c$ ($i\ne m$), $S+12B\sqrt{\ell c}\le Bc$, multiplies $\Phi$ by $1+\kappa/(8000B)$ unless $4S+q\le n/10$, and keeps $\{4S+q\le n/10\}$; the first round from $q=0$, $(1+\alpha)c_i\le c_m$ enters the invariant with $\Phi\ge n/(2k^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:pgood

nodes.statement: For the ratios: if $X\le tc/2$ one round cannot double it; if fewer than $n/20$ nodes are decided, $c$ grows by $16/9$, which absorbs the slack; otherwise $c\ge n/(20(1+B))$ and the deterministic drift $X\mu_m-\mu_Xc\ge\frac t2\kappa c^3/n$ beats the deviations, which needs $c^3\gtrsim n^2\log n$, i.e.\ $k\lesssim(n/\log n)^{1/3}$. For $\Phi$: $\mu_m+2\mu_q=n+(n-c-2q)^2/n+2W/n$ with $W=\sum_{j\ne m}c_j(c-c_j)\ge\kappa cS$ (the plurality drift, Lemma~1 of the paper). In the first round $q=0$, so the ratios square and $\mu_S=(\mathrm{md}-1)\mu_m$.

nodes.name: Plurality consensus
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha>0$ and $C=10^5((1+\alpha)^2/\alpha)^2$. For every $n$ with $\log n\ge C$, every $k$ with $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/3}$ and every configuration without undecided nodes in which colour $m$ has at least $1+\alpha$ times as many nodes as every other colour, all nodes hold $m$ after $\lceil C\,\mathrm{md}(x)\log n\rceil$ rounds with probability at least $1-6/n$ (SODA 2015, Theorem~11; the range of $k$ is discussed in \texttt{FORMALIZATION\_DIFFERENCES.md}).
nodes.label: thm:plurality

nodes.statement: One round into the invariant, then $T_2=\lceil\log(4k^2)/\log(1+\kappa/(8000B))\rceil\le 96000K\,\mathrm{md}\log n+1$ rounds with moving targets $\Phi\ge\frac n{2k^2}(1+\kappa/(8000B))^t$ or $4S+q\le n/10$, which end in $\{4S+q\le n/10\}$ since $\Phi\le n$; then $T_3=\lceil 8\log n\rceil$ rounds in which $4S+q$ contracts by $3/4$ in expectation. The failure probability is at most $T(k+4)/n^3+(3/4)^{T_3}n/10\le 6/n$.

nodes.name: Ratios and expectations
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{md}\le R\le k$ and $\mathrm{md}\le\Lambda\le k$; without undecided nodes $R=n/c_1$ and $\Lambda=n^2/\sum_ic_i^2$. With $\delta=q-n/2$: $\mu_i=(1+(2\delta+c_i)/n)\,c_i$ and $E[Q'-n/2]=(2\delta^2-\sum_jc_j^2)/n$ (the paper's (20) and (19)).
nodes.label: lem:lb-basic

nodes.statement: $c_i/c_1\in[0,1]$ gives $(c_i/c_1)^2\le c_i/c_1\le1$; Cauchy--Schwarz gives $R^2\le k\,\mathrm{md}$. The expectations are (3)--(4) rewritten with $q=n/2+\delta$.

nodes.name: First round; Lemma~3
nodes.statement: Let $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/2}$. From a configuration $x$ without undecided nodes, with plurality colour $m$, after one round, with probability at least $1-C/n$: $c_m\ge n/(2R^2)$, every colour has at most $2n/R^2$ nodes, and $n(1-2/\Lambda)\le q\le n(1-1/(2\Lambda))$ ($R$, $\Lambda$ of $x$).
nodes.label: lem:lb-first

nodes.statement: With $q=0$, $\mu_i=c_i^2/n\le\mu_m=n/R^2$ and $\mu_q=n-\sum_ic_i^2/n=n(1-1/\Lambda)$; in a good round (Lemma~\ref{lem:pgood}, deviation level $3\log n$) the deviations are small compared with $\mu_m\ge n/k^2\ge C^2\log n$ and with $n/\Lambda\ge n/k$. Proved with $C=100$.

nodes.name: Descent of the undecided nodes; Lemma~6
nodes.statement: Let $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/6}$. If $q=(1+\delta)n/2$ with $1-\delta\ge1/(2k)$, then after one round $Q'\le(1+\delta^2)n/2$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$ (16). If every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$, with $\gamma\ge1$ and $0<D\le k$, then $Q'\ge n/2-2\gamma^2n/D$ with probability at least $1-C/n^2$ (17, corrected). Hence there are $\gamma\ge1$ and $C$ such that, for $x$ without undecided nodes with $\mathrm{md}(x)\ge C$ and $y$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-first}, there is a round $t\le C\log n$ such that, with probability at least $1-C/n$, every colour is at most $\gamma n/\mathrm{md}(x)$ at each round $s\le t$, and at round $t$ also $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/\mathrm{md}(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:lb-descent

nodes.statement: (16): $\mu_q=(1+\delta^2)n/2-\sum_jc_j^2/n$ and $\sum_jc_j^2\ge(n-q)^2/k$. (17): $\mu_q\ge n/2-\sum_jc_j^2/n$ and $\sum_jc_j^2\le(\max_jc_j)(n-q)\le\gamma n^2/D$. The round $t$ is deterministic: the first $s$ with $(1-1/\Lambda)^{2^s}\le4\gamma^2/\mathrm{md}$. The colours follow an explicit envelope (at most $8n/D$, then at most $\gamma n/D$ with $\gamma=24$), iterated with moving targets. Proved with $\gamma=24$ and $C=10^6$.

nodes.name: Plateau; Lemma~7
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma\ge1$ and $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/4}$. If $C\le D\le k$, $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/D$ and every colour is at most $\gamma n/D$, then for every $T\le D/C$, after $T$ rounds, with probability at least $1-C/n$, every colour is at most $2\gamma n/D$ and $|q-n/2|\le2\gamma^2n/D$.
nodes.label: lem:lb-plateau

nodes.statement: One round multiplies the bound $B\in[\gamma n/D,2\gamma n/D]$ on the colours by at most $1+(4\gamma^2+2\gamma+1)/D$ and keeps the window, with probability at least $1-C/n^2$: by (20), $2\delta+c_i\le(4\gamma^2+2\gamma)n/D$, and by (19) $E[\Delta']\le 8\gamma^4n/D^2$ and $E[\Delta']\ge-(\max_jc_j)(n-q)/n\ge-(4\gamma/3)n/D$. Iterate for $T\le D/C$ rounds, during which the factor stays at most $2$. Proved with $C=30\gamma^2$.

nodes.name: Lower bound; Theorem~8
nodes.statement: There is $C>0$ such that, for every $n$ with $\log n\ge C$, every $k$ with $Ck\le(n/\log n)^{1/6}$ and every configuration $x$ without undecided nodes: for every $T$ with $CT\le\mathrm{md}(x)$, after $T$ rounds every colour has at most $Cn/\mathrm{md}(x)$ nodes with probability at least $1-C/n$; and for every $T$ with $C(T+1)\le\mathrm{md}(x)$, all nodes hold the same colour after $T$ rounds with probability at most $C/n$. Since monochromatic configurations are absorbing, the convergence time is $\Omega(\mathrm{md}(x))$ with probability at least $1-C/n$.
nodes.label: thm:lb

nodes.statement: Compose Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-first}, Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent} and Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-plateau} (with the $\gamma$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent}, $D=\mathrm{md}(x)$) by the Markov property; a round $T$ up to the descent round is covered by the bound at every round of Lemma~\ref{lem:lb-descent}. A monochromatic configuration has $n>Cn/\mathrm{md}(x)$ nodes of one colour once $\mathrm{md}(x)>C$. Proved with $C=1017429$ for the first form and $2C$ for the second.

nodes.name: Sequential undecided-state dynamics
nodes.statement: At each step an ordered pair (initiator, responder) of distinct agents is drawn uniformly among the $n(n-1)$ such pairs, independently of the past; only the responder updates, by the rule of Definition~\ref{def:usd} applied to the initiator's state. This is the approximate-majority protocol of Angluin, Aspnes and Eisenstat (Distributed Computing 21, 2008), with $x$, $y$ and blank written $a$, $b$ and $u$.
nodes.label: def:seq

nodes.name: One-step formula
nodes.statement: The expectation of a function of the next configuration that depends only on the states of the initiator and the responder is its value on idle interactions plus the four state-changing transitions $xb$, $yb$, $xy$, $yx$, weighted by $aq$, $bq$, $ab$, $ab$ pairs out of $n(n-1)$ (with $q$ the number of blank agents).
nodes.label: lem:seq-step

nodes.name: Weighted supermartingales
nodes.statement: If one step never increases $e^{\varphi}F$ in expectation, then $e^{\sum_{\text{path}}\varphi}F$ has expectation at most $F$ at every finite time, and Markov's inequality bounds the probability that the path sum of $\varphi$ is large.
nodes.label: lem:seq-mart

nodes.name: Six potentials
nodes.statement: The potentials $1/((a-b)^2+4n)$ (state-changing interactions), $1$ (central region), $1/(a+b)$ (blank corner), $3b+q+1$ and $3a+q+1$ (the two opinion corners), and $e^{-\lambda\max(a-b,0)}$ (the gap stays positive) satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:seq-mart} with suitable weights.
nodes.label: lem:seq-pot

nodes.name: Convergence; AAE Theorem 1
nodes.statement: For every $c$ there is $C$ such that from every non-blank configuration of $n\ge2$ agents, after $T\ge Cn\log n$ interactions all agents agree, with probability at least $1-C/n^c$.
nodes.label: thm:seq-conv

nodes.name: Correctness; AAE Theorem 2
nodes.statement: For every $c$ there is $C$ such that if initially $a-b\ge C\sqrt n\log n$, then after $T\ge Cn\log n$ interactions all agents hold $a$, with probability at least $1-C/n^c$.
nodes.label: thm:seq-maj

nodes.name: Finite weighted expectations
nodes.statement: A distribution has nonnegative real weights summing to one. A kernel is a family of such distributions, one for each state. Expectations are finite sums. These are shared library definitions, not numbered results of the paper.
nodes.label: def:weights

nodes.name: Stationary distribution exists
nodes.statement: Every finite nonempty stochastic matrix has a stationary distribution.
nodes.label: thm:stationary

nodes.statement: The shared library uses Ces\`aro averages of evolved distributions and compactness of the finite probability simplex. This supplies the existence fact recalled before Lemma 2.2; uniqueness is not required.

nodes.name: Finite-chain absorption
nodes.statement: An absorbing target accessible from every state of a finite chain admits a uniform positive success probability in a fixed number of rounds. The survival probability decays geometrically in blocks and tends to zero.
nodes.label: thm:generic-absorption

nodes.statement: Take a common block length exceeding all finitely many access times, then a maximum survival probability strictly below one. Iterate the resulting contraction.

nodes.name: Finite-horizon optional stopping
nodes.statement: If an observable equals $\varphi_A$ on $A$, $\varphi_B$ on $B$, lies in $[\varphi_B+m,\varphi_B+M]$ elsewhere, and keeps its expectation up to time $T$, then $\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_B-(\varphi_A-\varphi_B)\Pr(X_T\in A)$ lies between $m$ and $M$ times the probability of lying in neither event at time $T$.
nodes.label: thm:optional-stopping

nodes.statement: A shared library result (roadmap FND-4): decompose the observable pointwise into its values on $A$ and off $A\cup B$, take expectations, and bound the second part.

nodes.name: Synchronous copying
nodes.statement: A configuration is $s:V\to C$. Independently sample $r(i)$ according to row $H_i$, then set the next configuration to $i\mapsto s(r(i))$.
nodes.label: def:step

nodes.name: Configuration transition formula
nodes.statement: For configurations $s,t$, the transition probability is \[P_{st}=\prod_i\sum_{j:s(j)=t(i)}H_{ij}.\] For Boolean colors a white target vertex contributes $\sum_j H_{ij}s(j)$; a black target contributes its complement, giving the paper's product formula.
nodes.label: lem:product

nodes.statement: The configuration distribution is the pushforward of the independently sampled neighbors. Factor its equality indicator into a product over vertices.

nodes.name: Monochromatic-edge propagation
nodes.statement: On a connected nonbipartite graph every Boolean configuration has a possible finite path to a constant configuration.
nodes.label: lem:propagation

nodes.statement: A coloring without a monochromatic edge would be a proper two-coloring. Starting with a monochromatic edge, each vertex of its region can keep that color by sampling an internal neighbor. Connectedness supplies an edge leaving every proper region. One more vertex can copy across that edge. Induction on the number of vertices outside the region gives consensus.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1: absorption
nodes.statement: Assume $H_{ij}>0$ whenever $i,j$ are adjacent; extra support, such as self-loops, is allowed. Both constant configurations are absorbing, and the probability of remaining nonconstant tends to zero. This is the finite-time survival formulation of the paper's transience claim.
nodes.label: lem:21

nodes.statement: Every possible copying round has positive probability. Thus graph propagation gives accessibility. Apply the shared finite-chain absorption theorem.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.3: invariant stationary weight
nodes.statement: For any stationary distribution $\pi$, the expected white mass at every finite time is the initial mass $\sum_i\pi_i s(i)$. No graph connectivity assumption is imposed on this invariant.
nodes.label: lem:23

nodes.statement: A vertex's expected next color indicator is $\sum_jH_{ij}s(j)$. Interchanging finite sums and using $\pi H=\pi$ proves one-step preservation; induction proves the iterated statement.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.2: limiting identification
nodes.statement: The discrepancy between expected stationary white mass and all-white probability lies between zero and nonconsensus probability. Consequently all-white probability converges to initial stationary white mass. The implementation combines the paper's limiting identification with the invariant from Lemma 2.3 when stating the limit.
nodes.label: lem:22

nodes.statement: Pointwise, the white mass agrees with the all-white indicator on constant configurations and lies in $[0,1]$ elsewhere. Finite-horizon optional stopping, with the two consensus configurations as targets and the invariant of Lemma 2.3, bounds the discrepancy; squeeze it using Lemma 2.1.

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Define eventual all-white probability as the supremum of the increasing finite-time all-white probabilities. It equals the initial stationary white mass.
nodes.label: thm:21

nodes.statement: Consensus is absorbing, so the probabilities increase and are bounded by one. Their supremum is their limit. Identify this limit using Lemma 2.2.

nodes.name: Corollary 2.2 and regular graphs
nodes.statement: For uniform neighbor sampling, $\pi_i=d_i/(2|E|)$, so all-white consensus has probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=1}d_i/(2|E|)$. On a regular graph this is the initial fraction of white vertices.
nodes.label: cor:22

nodes.statement: The degree-sum formula normalizes these weights. In the stationarity equation, the degree cancels the reciprocal sampling degree; undirected adjacency gives the remaining column sum. Equal degrees then give uniform vertex weights.

nodes.name: Consensus in a specified color
nodes.statement: For a finite color set and any specified color $c$, its eventual consensus probability is $\sum_{i:s(i)=c}\pi_i$. These probabilities sum to one.
nodes.label: thm:colors

nodes.statement: The color-indicator projection commutes with every copying step and with iterated expectations. Its all-white event is exactly all-$c$ consensus. Apply Theorem 2.1 to this Boolean projection.

nodes.name: Rounds, backward map, Wright--Fisher sampling
nodes.statement: A run applies rounds $r_1,\dots,r_T\colon V\to V$ in order. Its backward map is $r_1\circ r_2\circ\cdots\circ r_T$. The disagreement indicator is $0$ on constant configurations and $1$ otherwise. Wright--Fisher sampling picks every row uniformly on $V$, self included, i.e.\ the complete graph with self-loops.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: def:backward

nodes.name: Duality with coalescing walks
nodes.statement: After rounds $r_1,\dots,r_T$ the configuration is $s\circ r_1\circ\cdots\circ r_T$: running the voter forward reads the initial colours through the backward map, whose point images are coalescing random walks. If the backward map is constant, the configuration is a consensus.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: lem:duality

nodes.statement: Induction on the list of rounds, since one round maps $s$ to $s\circ r$.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Rounds are independent and uniform
nodes.statement: Under Wright--Fisher sampling a round is uniform on $V\to V$, so the $T$-step configuration kernel is the average over $T$ independent uniform rounds.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: lem:wf-rounds

nodes.statement: The product weights are all $n^{-n}$; induct on $T$, peeling off the first round.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Meeting probability
nodes.statement: Two coordinates of a uniform map $V\to V$ agree with probability $1/n$. Hence the backward walks from two distinct vertices have not met after $T$ rounds with probability exactly $(1-1/n)^T$.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: lem:meeting

nodes.statement: Peel off the first round, swap it with the remaining average, and multiply by the one-round probability of not meeting; induct on $T$.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Consensus time
nodes.statement: The probability that no consensus is reached after $T$ rounds is at most $(n-1)(1-1/n)^T$. Consequently consensus is reached within $2n\log n$ rounds with probability at least $1-1/n$.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time
nodes.label: thm:consensus-time

nodes.statement: Consensus holds once every backward walk has met the walk of a fixed vertex; apply the union bound over the other $n-1$ vertices and the meeting probability, then $(1-1/n)^T\le e^{-T/n}\le n^{-2}$ for $T\ge 2n\log n$.
nodes.section: 87 Section 2.4 on the complete graph: coalescing walks and consensus time

nodes.name: Propagation through the kernel support
nodes.statement: Call a round possible for $H$ when every vertex samples a vertex of positive weight in its row. On a connected graph whose edges are charged by $H$, a monochromatic region in which every vertex charges a vertex of the region grows to consensus through possible rounds. If $H_{vv}>0$ for one vertex $v$, the region $\{v\}$ qualifies, so nonconsensus probability tends to zero, bipartite graphs included.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: lem:kernel-propagation

nodes.statement: As in Lemma~2.1: a boundary vertex copies its neighbour in the region, vertices of the region copy inside it, and all other vertices copy any vertex of positive weight. Possible rounds have positive probability, and the finite-chain absorption theorem applies.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Remark, p.~254
nodes.statement: On a connected graph, bipartite or not, if $H$ charges every edge and $H_{vv}>0$ for some vertex $v$, then consensus in colour $c$ has probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=c}\pi_i$ for every stationary $\pi$.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: thm:selfloop

nodes.statement: Lemma~2.2 only needs nonconsensus probability to vanish; then project colours as in Section~2.3.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Lazy voter
nodes.statement: The lazy kernel $(I+H)/2$ has the stationary distributions of $H$ and positive self-loops. On any connected graph the lazy voter $(I+D^{-1}A)/2$ reaches consensus in colour $c$ with probability $\sum_{i:s(i)=c} d_i/2m$.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: thm:lazy

nodes.statement: Apply the Remark to $(I+H)/2$; for uniform neighbour sampling use the degree distribution.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Neutral Wright--Fisher fixation
nodes.statement: If every offspring picks a uniform parent, itself included, allele $a$ fixes with probability $c_a/n$, where $c_a$ is its initial number of copies.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)
nodes.label: thm:wright-fisher

nodes.statement: The uniform distribution is stationary and every entry is positive. For $n\ge 3$ the complete graph is nonbipartite and Section~2.3 applies; for every $n$ the Remark applies.
nodes.section: 88 Self-loops, the lazy voter and Wright--Fisher (VOT-2)

nodes.name: Two-token walk, lazy sampling
nodes.statement: For a sampling kernel $H$, two tokens move with the rounds of the voter dynamics: the token at $x$ moves to $r(x)$, where $r$ is drawn from the independent product of the rows of $H$.
